children.name: Planguage
children.definition: **Planguage** (*030) is a specification language and a set of related methods for systems engineering. It specifically supports requirement specification, design specification, design impact analysis, specification quality control, and evolutionary project management.

children.name: Requirement
children.definition: A 'requirement' is a **stakeholder-valued system state, under stated conditions.**

children.name: Resource
children.definition: A **resource** is any potential system input. It is any kind of input 'fuel' necessary for building, operating or maintaining a given system. A resource is an asset or a supply that can be used to produce the functionality, or performance levels, of a system.

children.name: Role
children.definition:
A **Role** is a defined responsibility, interest or scope for people. More fully, a Role is:
- A defined Process, carried out by Defined Actors, with Defined Skills, acting according to Defined Rules, for Defined Purposes, with a Defined Responsibility, and a Defined Duration, le

children.name: Strategy
children.definition: A **strategy** is any 'means' specified with the intent to impact defined objectives.

children.name: Agent
children.definition: Any combination of person, group, and/or machine, which carries out a defined (written) procedure, thus doing a task, which is a part of a process (other parts being entry and exit sub-processes).

children.name: Define
children.definition: To **define** is to officially explain a specified concept in writing.

children.name: Generate
children.definition: 'Generate' is a relationship concept. It relates things that produce other things. Keyed icon: 'A { B' means 'A Generates B'. There is an implication that the Generator (A) continues to exist after it has generated ({) something (B).

children.name: Mechanism
children.definition:
"A system of mutually adapted parts working together as … a means by which a particular effect is produced."
In Planguage: a **Mechanism** is HOW the system does a function ("means"). Don Mills (NZ, 2002) articulated the four-level WHY/WHAT/HOW/HOW structure: *Providing the servi

children.name: Service
children.definition: A **service** is the provision of a facility to meet the needs or for the use of a person or thing (Oxford English Dictionary). In Planguage terms, providing the service is *why* a system does something — the purpose that a function exists to fulfil.

children.name: Parameter Value
children.definition: The parameter value is a numeric value, which varies along a defined scale, and which specifies the meaning of a given parameter.

children.name: Quantity
children.definition: A **Quantity** describes 'How much' a system performs or consumes. A quantity is an attribute measured in terms of Capacity (*459) or Resources (*199). A 'quantity' is a type of attribute which we would not normally call a 'quality' (*125). All system quantities can have quality

children.name: Architectural Description
children.definition: Architectural description is "a collection of products to *document* an architecture."

children.name: Architecture
children.definition:
The 'architecture' is the set of entities that:
- in fact exist and impact a set of system attributes directly,
- or indirectly, by
- constraining, or influencing, related engineering decisions.

children.name: Infotecture
children.definition: Infotecture is a discipline practised by Infotects (*568). It is information systems architecture. Infotecture is a specialised architecture discipline limited to information systems of any kind, and not necessarily including computers or software!

children.name: Softecture
children.definition: **Softecture** is a concatenation of *software* and *architecture* — the highest level of design activity in a software engineering project, or in the software area of a systems engineering activity.

children.name: Systems Architecture
children.definition: **Systems Architecture** is the set of artifacts produced by Architecture Engineering. A systems architecture is a strategic framework and consists of models, standards and design constraints specifying mandatory and recommended best practice for implementing and maintaining syst

children.name: Editor
children.definition:
During the Edit sub-process of SQC, an 'editor' is a person who evaluates issues (and other Editor Advice Log information) and takes appropriate action on them.
**Note:** The appropriate action might include correcting something if the issues are defects, or sending change reques

children.name: Scribe
children.definition: The **scribe** writes up the Editor Advice Log or other team notes during an SQC (Software Quality Control) meeting — capturing editorial advice and decisions so they are not lost after the meeting ends.

children.name: Specification Writer
children.definition: A **Specification Writer** is the person responsible for articulating, composing, and maintaining a specification — translating stakeholder needs, engineering decisions, and system requirements into formal, written Planguage specifications. Synonyms: Author, spec writer, cognizan

children.name: Authority
children.definition: Authority is a specific level of power to 'decide' or 'influence' or 'enforce' a specific matter requiring some degree of judgment or evaluation. For example, the status of a specification is usually the responsibility of some 'authority' (some set of individuals holding the spec

children.name: Owner
children.definition: An **Owner** is a person or group responsible for an object, and for authorising any change to it.

children.name: Process Change Management Team
children.definition: A Process Change Management Team is a team responsible for managing and governing changes to defined processes in an engineering or development organisation.

children.name: Responsible
children.definition: **Responsible** is the person or instance assigned formal responsibility for achieving a specified plan element.

children.name: Team Leader
children.definition: A **Team Leader** is responsible for managing a specification quality control (SQC) process.

children.name: Chance Cause
children.definition: Synonym of Special Cause "Special Cause" (*019).

children.name: Root Causes
children.definition: **Root Causes** are the ultimate upstream reason why an error/defect/fault/malfunction sequence occurs. Rationale: Root causes are interesting because by identifying them you will generally have identified the most efficient points for change to prevent downstream problems.

children.name: Business Level
children.definition: Business Level is the topmost layer of the Value Delivery Tree. It expresses what the Business stakeholder values: profit, market position, growth, sustainability, regulatory compliance. Business outcomes are the effects produced by everything below; they are the ultimate justifi

children.name: Essential Objective
children.definition: Essential objectives are the ones which are capable of influencing the Fundamental objective when they are reached or implemented. Compare with 'Controllable'.

children.name: Evo Level
children.definition: Evo Level is the smallest unit of value-delivering work, sized to fit a single evolutionary delivery cycle (typically 1-2 weeks). Multiple Evo deliveries integrate to form a Solution. Evo deliveries are the operational, day-to-day cause whose accumulated effect is Solution.

children.name: Fundamental Objective
children.definition: Fundamental Objectives are 'givens'. They are what we are trying to support and impact by reaching 'strategic objectives'. They form the top level of a relative hierarchy of objectives. They are the given objectives handed down to 'us' from above.

children.name: Kid
children.definition: The kid is the immediate offspring or subset of any component type with any sub-components (for example, function, process, plan, step or system).

children.name: Product Level
children.definition: Product Level is the layer where products and services are described as functions and qualities. Products are the output that stakeholders consume to satisfy their needs. Product requirements quantify the Functions and Qualities the Solutions must deliver.

children.name: Solution Level
children.definition: Solution Level is the layer where implementation choices (Designs, Strategies, Means) are specified. Solutions are the means by which Products are realised. Solutions create Product effects; they are the cause whose effect is Product.

children.name: Stakeholder Level
children.definition: Stakeholder Level is the layer where each stakeholder group's needs and values are quantified. Stakeholders consume Products; what they value rolls up to create Business value. Stakeholder requirements are expressed as quantified values on scales.

children.name: Strategic Objective
children.definition: **Strategic Objectives** are the objectives which are our main responsibility. They support fundamental objectives and are themselves supported by means objectives.

children.name: Artifact
children.definition: Development artifacts are engineering information and tools such as specifications, test cases, user documentation which are not regarded as product components, but can potentially be reused to develop products and product components.

children.name: Artifact
children.definition: A collective term for all Planguage "Planguage" {books, slides, translations, variants, dialects, and other related things}.

children.name: Asset
children.definition: An asset is a potential resource.

children.name: Attached Specification
children.definition: Attached specifications are directly and visibly present specification elements to one given specification.

children.name: Benchmark Cost
children.definition: A benchmark cost is an expenditure of resource that has been determined by some means for purposes of comparison and analysis.

children.name: Binding
children.definition: A formal engineering decision type which constrains variability of product line artifacts or components in order to improve the potential for reuse and commonality.

children.name: Budget Target
children.definition: A Budget Target is a numeric resource-expenditure allocation plan. They are expressed with target levels {Budget, Wish, Stretch}.

children.name: Cell
children.definition: In an Impact Estimation table, a cell is an intersection between a requirement attribute (usually a performance or a resource/cost attribute) and a design idea.

children.name: Content
children.definition:
Content is the meaning or message contained in a specification as distinct from its appearance, form, or style.
Actual specification content may or may not totally reflect a concept we have in mind. It might intentionally simplify the concept, or specify a particular view of it.

children.name: Entity
children.definition: Entities exist. An entity is a real thing. An entity is real in the sense that it has provable existence, and it has performance and cost attributes. An entity can be natural or human made. It can be conceptual or physical.

children.name: Feature
children.definition:
A feature is a class of stakeholder perceptible characteristics of a system, which are useful for comparing against competitive product, service or system benchmarks.
The point being to help stakeholders see that this system is equal, better or different from others. A feature ca

children.name: Implementation Instance
children.definition: An Implementation Instance is a particular real-life representation of an idea. Possibly one of many planned, implemented, or obsolete.

children.name: Interface
children.definition: An interface is an agreed connection and boundary between system components.

children.name: Materials
children.definition: **Materials** are non-information process-inputs and process-outputs.

children.name: Object
children.definition:
An object is any system component that can be described in terms of its attributes; functions, *performance, and cost*; as well as past, present or future attribute states.
An object can be real or conceptual. It is a term we use for systematic building blocks of larger systems —

children.name: Symmetry
children.definition: Explicit pairing of downside protection with upside capture rights. Downside Limit = Tolerable (we already have this). Upside Capture = Monster (new).

children.name: Specification Language
children.definition: **Specification Language** provides the structures and formats used to express Planguage specifications. Its formal skeleton — Planguage parameters, icons, concept definitions, and specification conventions — is the framework onto which product language is integrated.

children.name: Design Constraint
children.definition:
A design constraint is an explicit and direct restriction regarding the choice of design ideas. It either declares a design idea to be compulsory (**Mandatory Design**) or to be excluded (**Prohibited Design**).
Design constraints are dictated from an earlier system development s

children.name: Scalar Constraint
children.keyedIcon: [ and ] and >> (Fail), and others as per specializations list
children.definition: A **Scalar Constraint** is some kind of limitation on the delivered level of a defined Scale of Measure. It marks regions on the scale that must not be entered — or must not be exceeded — under penalty of failure, unacceptability, or catastrophe.

children.name: Binary Constraint
children.definition: A Binary Constraint is a constraint that only has two possible status conditions: complied with or not.

children.name: Budget Constraint
children.definition: *\<this was found missing, and is messy in other terms, check all \*421\> tg*

children.name: Budget Cycle Constraint
children.definition: A restriction regarding budget, which is related to the budget cycle process, such as when, who, how much.

children.name: Condition Constraint
children.definition:
A condition constraint is a requirement that *imposes a conscious restriction* for a specified system scope.
A condition constraint, also called a 'restriction,' is a binary type of requirement.

children.name: Cycle-Constraint
children.definition: A planning constraint on an evolutionary project cycle of any kind. Typically expressed in a planning policy, and requiring a cycle to be planned within certain time or financial limits.

children.name: Veto Constraint
children.definition: A **veto** is a negative constraint; the type 'Don't do X'.

children.name: Demand Constraint
children.definition: A demand is a constraint of type 'You must do X'. It is a non-scalar, affirmative constraint — it mandates a specific behaviour, action, or condition, rather than setting a numeric limit.

children.name: Derived Constraint
children.definition: A specific local constraint derived from a Generic 'template' Constraint or Global 'wide scope' Constraint.

children.name: Direct Constraint
children.definition: Any constraint which is specified in the *format of a constraint*, and is intended to directly constrain performance, function, costs or design.

children.name: Fundamental Constraints
children.definition: A 'given'. Fundamental Constraints are constraints that are handed down to us from higher authority. They are fundamental if we choose not to question them, but to heed them without question or alteration.

children.name: Indirect Constraint
children.definition:
Any *other specification, except a direct constraint,* which indirectly has the effect of constraint.
This can include any other requirement {function, Goal, Wish, Stretch}, and previous and pre-emptive level of architecture or design, and any statement of priority attached to a

children.name: Engineering Constraint
children.definition: An engineering constraint is a constraint on the engineering process itself, rather than on the product.

children.name: Environment Constraint
children.definition: An Environment Constraint is any system constraint that is not a focus system constraint. Environment constraints are particularly intended to describe constraints on the life cycle of a product or system, such as design and architecture phases, construction and acquisition phase

children.name: Function Constraint
children.definition:
A **function constraint** is a requirement which places a restriction on the functionality that may exist in a system.
A function constraint is binary: it specifies that a specific function must be, or must not be, present. The implication is that some kind of failure will result

children.name: Means Constraints
children.definition: **Means Constraints** are constraints imposed at levels 'below' and supporting us. This means that we can therefore overrule means constraints, if we need to in order to better satisfy our strategic requirements.

children.name: Product Constraint
children.definition: Product Constraints are constraints that apply to the process output of an engineering process: the product or system being made by it.

children.name: Constraint Attribute
children.definition: A constraint can possess a number of potentially interesting attributes. Analysis of these Constraint Attributes can help us understand the full consequences of a particular constraint specification earlier, perhaps avoiding unnecessary negative consequences.

children.name: Generic Constraint
children.definition: A Generic Constraint applies to a defined scope. It is tailored in interpretation or specification at the detailed level.

children.name: Result Constraint
children.definition: A **Result Constraint** is a term for a requirements constraint used for any of the requirement types: quality, cost, or Function. It is used where we do not wish to be more specific about the specific type of constraint. The term 'result' refers to any combination of performance

children.name: Strategic Constraints
children.definition: **Strategic Constraints** are constraints we have imposed at our own level, over which we have control.

children.name: Cost
children.definition: Cost is an *expense* incurred in building or maintaining a system. It is consumption of a resource.

children.name: Indirect Costs
children.definition: A resource (money, time, work-hours) needed to produce an *input* to a system.

children.name: Price of Nonconformance
children.definition: The **Price of Nonconformance (PONC)** is "What it costs to do things wrong" [CROSBY85]. PONC is the cost to find and fix defects between two defined points in a systems engineering development process — including reprocessing, rework, scrap, warranty, downtime, and all other cos

children.name: Cost, to
children.definition: To 'cost' something is specifically to estimate the *resources* needed to achieve a planned set of requirements. To estimate costs.

children.name: To Budget
children.definition: **'To budget'** refers to a process to plan the allocation of limited resources to a system. The budgeting process results in the specification of a set of target and constraint specifications for one or more resources.

children.name: Trigger
children.definition: A **Trigger** is a quantified early-warning signal that the monster is approaching, defined while we still have time to re-allocate resources.

children.name: Bug
children.definition:
A **Bug** is a defect in a real system which, if *provoked* by an agent or specific data, can result in a system [[Malfunction.275|Malfunction]].
*Fault* is a synonym for Bug; in Planguage both terms name the same concept at *339.

children.name: Specification Defect
children.definition: A **Specification Defect** is any error, omission, ambiguity, inconsistency, or rule violation found in a specification document. It is a defect in the *specification itself* — not in the code, system, or product — and is the primary target of the [[Defect-Detection-Process.041|D

children.name: Error
children.definition: An 'error' is something done incorrectly by a human being. Errors are usually committed unintentionally; they are often forced to happen by 'bad' work processes (Statistical Process Control Theory [DEMING86, JURAN64 &74]).

children.name: Issue
children.definition: An issue is any subject of concern that needs to be noted for analysis and resolution.

children.name: Major Defect
children.definition: A Major defect is a specification defect (a rule violation), which if not fixed at an early stage of specification, then its consequences will possibly grow substantially, in cost-to-fix and/or damage potential. A Major defect has on average approximately an order of magnitude mo

children.name: Malfunction
children.definition: A system has a 'malfunction' when it does something not intended, or not desired, according to its design/construction specification, or according to reasonable stakeholder expectations (even though there may be no official specification about that expectation). *Malfunctions are

children.name: Minor Defect
children.definition: A minor defect is a non-major defect. It has no major downstream cost potential.

children.name: Non-Commentary
children.definition: 'Non-commentary' refers to written specification that is not commentary: it is either core specification or background specification. All major specification defects are found in non-commentary. But, not all specification defects in non-commentary specifications are major. By def

children.name: Specification Issue
children.definition: A **Specification Issue** is a checker-perceived potential defect in any form of documentation or system development specification. When resolved by the author or editor, a specification issue either becomes an acknowledged defect or is dismissed.

children.name: Clarity
children.definition: The specification quality of 'being understood by a defined readership as intended by the writer'.

children.name: Cumulative Defect Removal Effectiveness
children.definition: The cumulative defect-removal percentage of a defined series of defect-removal processes. For example, a series of specification defect-removal stages, plus various testing stages.

children.name: Estimated Remaining Defects
children.definition:
This is an estimate of defect density remaining in a specification at any given time.
The estimate is based on defects found (using knowledge of % defect-finding effectiveness) and defects attempted removed (using knowledge of % effectiveness of the correction process). The defec

children.name: Fix Probability
children.definition: The Fix Probability is the probability that an attempt to correct (fix) a specification defect, or system fault, will succeed.

children.name: Specification Quality Level
children.definition: The **Specification Quality Level** is a measure of a specification's conformance to any specified relevant standards. Operationally, it is the estimated number of remaining major defects per logical page — the primary output metric of the SQC process.

children.name: Process Improvement
children.definition: The systematic activity of determining the root systemic causes of human work process problems, then changing defined and stable work processes, so as to eliminate, or reduce, the human tendency to commit errors; and to thus improve productivity or costs.

children.name: Process Meeting
children.definition: A process meeting is an SQC sub-process. It is part of the SQC Defect Prevention Process (DPP).

children.name: Comment
children.definition: See Note *018.

children.name: Description
children.definition:
A description is a set of words and/or diagrams that describe, and *partially* define, a component.
The parameter 'Description' (or synonyms Detail, Detailed Description) is used to specify description.

children.name: Expression Quotes
children.definition:
Expression quotes are 'single quotes' at the beginning and end of an expression. They are used to make it clear that this is a *single* expression, using a set of related terms.
*Rationale:* They are useful when the expression is complicated and some doubt could arise as to the e

children.name: Expression
children.definition:
A Planguage 'expression' is part or all of a Planguage 'statement': it is one or more related Planguage components of any kind.
Expressions are defined by one or more Planguage terms.
Expressions are comprised of Planguage language concepts. These concepts include: {parameters, i

children.name: Generic Term
children.definition: A generic term is a Term in a Specification that needs further definition, there or elsewhere.

children.name: Gist
children.definition: A Gist parameter is used to state the essence, or main point, of a specification. A Gist is a summary of the detailed specification.

children.name: Grammar
children.definition: Implicit: Planguage grammar. The system of rules used by Planguage users to form statements and larger constructions or relations from Planguage elements. The rules for Planguage.

children.name: Parameter Definition
children.definition: A **parameter definition** is a set of words defining the parameter. It is a parameter specification.

children.name: Parameter Specification
children.definition: A **parameter specification** is either the 'Parameter Definition', or the 'Parameter Value'. It generally comes after the parameter name, after any [qualifier], and before any source information.

children.name: Planguage Term
children.definition: A **Planguage Term** (*211) is any concept name that is defined as being part of Planguage.

children.name: Relative Specification
children.definition: A 'relative' specification is a Planguage specification where the exact interpretation is dependent on the meaning of one or more other specifications.

children.name: Specification Variable
children.definition: A **Specification Variable** is any term in a specification which references another term — whose definition we must look up in order to interpret the specification. The variable's value is not fixed; it can be resolved differently depending on time, context, or an external agree

children.name: Specification
children.definition: A **specification** communicates one or more system ideas and/or descriptions to an intended audience. A specification is a formal, written means for communicating information. It can address requirements (what the system must achieve), design ideas (how it will be achieved), con

children.name: Statement
children.definition: A **statement** is one or more Planguage expressions connected to form a meaningful and complete specification. Numerous classes of Planguage statement exist, including: Requirement, Design, Plan, Relationship, Note, Parameter, Condition, and Function.

children.name: Symbology
children.definition: The system of symbols representing ideas, which includes {terminology, icons, symbols}.

children.name: Term
children.definition: A **Planguage Term** is a minimum set of words and/or symbols (icons) that has a defined Planguage meaning.

children.name: User-Defined Term
children.definition: In Planguage, a **user-defined term** is a definition of a term made by a Planguage user. It is not a Planguage term (like Scale or Goal), nor a customer-tailored Planguage term, such as a new Parameter, Parameter Synonym or grammatical variation.

children.name: Alternative Designs
children.definition: Alternative designs will have satisfactory, but *different*, performance and cost attributes. The alternative design idea attributes will be so significant that they do not need any *other* alternative design ideas in addition, or cannot afford it.

children.name: Definition
children.definition: **Definition** (or **Defined As**) is a parameter that is used to define a tagged term. The tagged term can then be re-used anywhere else within scope, and will always carry this precise definition. The keyed icons are `:` (primary) or `=` (less common).

children.name: Design Specification
children.definition:
A design specification is the written specification of a design idea.
A set of design specifications is the main output of a design engineering process.
A specific set of design specifications, when implemented, will, to some degree, meet the stated requirements.

children.name: Design Target
children.definition: A Design Target is the specific target *level*, including *qualifier*, of an attribute requirement that is being worked towards, in the design or implementation process.

children.name: Function Design
children.definition:
**Function design** is a design primarily aimed at satisfying specified function requirements.
A specified function design has two characteristics, which we primarily select it for:
- function requirement satisfaction, and
- satisfactory consequent levels of performance and cost

children.name: Idea
children.definition:
An 'idea' is an intellectual concept of any kind.
*Webster's Dictionary:* A plan, scheme, project, aim.
*American Heritage Dictionary:* A plan, scheme, or method.

children.name: Performance Design
children.definition: Performance Design is design specification aimed at, or as a side effect, satisfying performance level requirements. By definition this includes capacity requirements, quality requirements and savings requirements.

children.name: Specific Design
children.definition: A **specific design** is a precise and definite design, intended to give the final range of performance and cost attributes resulting from that design to a real system. It is distinct from all upstream design notions, which are intended to narrow choices in an appropriate directi

children.name: Specify, To
children.definition: To **specify** means to articulate an idea. Specifying can be done in writing or orally, using text and/or symbols. In Planguage, specifying typically refers to the act of producing a formal, structured written specification — but oral specification (e.g., capturing stakeholder n

children.name: Supplementary Designs
children.definition: **Supplementary Designs** are needed to move the set of designs towards the design Goal levels, other target levels, or towards meeting other requirements (constraints, functions).

children.name: Constraint Design
children.definition: Constraint Design is design specification aimed at, or as a side effect, satisfying Constraint requirements.

children.name: Core Specification
children.definition: Anything classed as 'core specification' will result in real system changes being made: incorrect core specification would materially and negatively affect the system in terms of costs, effort, or quality. Specification defects in core specification are almost always of major sev

children.name: Specification Constant
children.definition: A **specification constant** is a Tag in a specification which always translates to a specific, stable definition. The definition might be updated or improved over time, but it does not vary as a function of time or external environment. It is the stable counterpart to a Specific

children.name: Time Cycle Constraint
children.definition: In Evo delivery cycle planning, the **Time Cycle Constraint** is the maximum-recommended duration of a Frontroom delivery cycle (as opposed to a result cycle). The average duration time that a customer has to wait for a delivery.

children.name: Creativity
children.definition:
The process of identifying, defining, and evaluating ideas, with respect to defined criteria.
The *degree* of creativity is the degree of effects on defined performance requirements, and on defined constraints.

children.name: Design Engineering
children.definition:
Design Engineering is an iterative process of determining a set of designs, with rigorous attention to quantified and measurable control of their impact on requirements.
The design engineering process implies the matching of potential and specified design ideas with quantified pe

children.name: Design To Cost
children.definition: 'Design To Cost' is an engineering strategy of consciously selecting design ideas, which will allow you to stay within any and all resource budgets.

children.name: Optimize
children.definition: To **optimize** a design ("design optimization") is to reduce one or more resources needed to achieve specified levels of performance or stakeholder values — or to improve the impact of designs in the direction of specified performance targets.

children.name: Case
children.definition: Cases are real or doctored-for-discretion (originally real) examples of practice of Planguage (this method).

children.name: Effort
children.keyedIcon: resource icon with benchmark and target icons
children.definition:
Human-energy task cost. The human resources needed to accomplish something.
Scale of measure: the defined [type of effort, default = engineering hours] needed to accomplish a defined [task].

children.name: Process Improvement Effort
children.definition: The Resources used to improve a work Process.

children.name: Work Hours
children.definition: **Work Hours** is the total hours of work, irrespective of clock-hours, or number of people involved. The cost of doing something.

children.name: Architecture Engineering
children.definition: The architecture engineering process puts in place the systems architecture, which is a controlling mechanism for the design engineering of any project.

children.name: Competitive Engineering
children.definition: A Systems Engineering discipline that is focused on 'winning', relative to some competitor, some enemy, some challenges, some events, or some Benchmarks.

children.name: Continuous Process Improvement
children.definition: Continuous Process Improvement (CPI) includes any and all continuous long-term effort to systematically improve an organisation's work processes.

children.name: Engineering
children.definition: Engineering is an Evolutionary Process, using practical Principles, in order to determine, and identify the Means to deliver, the best achievable Performance and Cost levels balance, for optimal Stakeholder satisfaction, in a complex risk-filled environment.

children.name: Software Engineering
children.definition: **Software Engineering** is the engineering discipline of enabling and motivating software systems to deliver a balanced set of values, directly or indirectly, to a balanced set of stakeholders, throughout their lifecycle.

children.name: Systems Engineering
children.definition: **Systems Engineering (SE)** is an engineering process, encompassing and managing all relevant system stakeholders requirements; as well as all design solutions; and necessary technology, economic, and political areas.

children.name: Designer
children.definition: A designer is a person or group who specifies design ideas, in an effort to satisfy specified requirements.

children.name: Infotect
children.definition: The Infotect is: (1) Information systems architect. (2) Responsible for all aspects of the system — manual procedures, people, training, documentation, motivation — and if they are used at all, both hardware and software, including dataware. (3) Goal oriented: the infotect's job

children.name: Producer
children.definition: A 'producer' is the agent or process, which generates product from a process. One class of producer is 'author', who is a producer of written products as opposed to non-written products. Producers make products for customers and users.

children.name: Softcrafter
children.definition: A **Softcrafter** is a person who practices the craft of programming software for computers — commonly known as a programmer or coder.

children.name: Software Engineer
children.definition: A **Software Engineer** is an engineer with specialty in software — characterised by the ability to assemble software components based on quantified attributes, meeting multiple quantified requirement performance levels within specified resource constraints.

children.name: Systems Architect
children.definition: A **systems architect** is a person or group, who carries out the work tasks of systems architecture (a process).

children.name: Systems Engineer
children.definition: One who practices systems engineering (*223) or is qualified to do so.

children.name: Estimate
children.definition: An estimate is a numeric judgment about a future, present or past level of a scalar system attribute. This includes all performance and cost attributes. Estimates are usually made where direct measurement is impossible (future), impractical (past), or uneconomic (current levels).

children.name: Gap
children.definition: For a scalar attribute, a Gap is the range from either an impact estimate, or a specific Benchmark (usually the current level), to a specific target (or occasionally, to a specific constraint).

children.name: Ideal
children.definition: An **Ideal** specification represents a hypothetical, and perhaps only theoretical, best level for stakeholders, irrespective of considerations such as cost, available technology, or culture. An Ideal parameter specifies an ideal level, on a defined Scale, under specified conditi

children.name: Need
children.definition:
A 'need' is something desired by a defined stakeholder.
The implication is that satisfying that need would have some value for some stakeholder.
A need might not be agreed as a formal requirement, and it might not be prioritized such that it is actually acted upon (designed and i

children.name: Path Plan
children.definition: A Path Plan is a series of two or more specified levels on a defined scale of measure from defined optional Benchmark levels and including any interesting series of defined constraint and Target levels. The path plan can be used to specify any interesting planned set of intermedi

children.name: Percentage Impact
children.definition:
A percentage impact is an incremental scale impact expressed as a percentage of the required improvement (The required improvement being the scalar distance between a chosen benchmark (0%) and a chosen target (100%)).
A percentage impact is part of an impact estimate and is used

children.name: Perfect
children.definition: A 'perfect' level of an attribute is a level that is flawless, complete and without defect of any kind. It cannot ever be improved under any circumstances. It is a benchmark concept.

children.name: Progress
children.definition: Progress is scalar-requirement movement, from benchmarks towards desired and intended levels, like targets and constraints.

children.name: Real Values
children.definition: Real values are estimates in impact estimation based on the 'real' defined Scale of measure.

children.name: Regress
children.definition: Regress refers to a scalar level that is worse than a defined benchmark.

children.name: Result
children.definition: A **Result** is an outcome for a system after — or the 'testable effect of' — the 'Do' phase of any Plan Do Study Act (PDSA) cycle. Results are analysed in the 'Study' phase. Within Evo, 'result' is specifically used to refer to any outcome of a delivery cycle within a result cyc

children.name: Variability
children.definition: Any development artifacts or components that do not have identical corresponding artifacts in another product represent **variability** between the products.

children.name: Assumption
children.definition: Assumptions are unproven conditions, which if not true at some defined point in time, would threaten something, such as the validity of a specification or the achievement of our requirements.

children.name: Background
children.definition: Background information is the part of a specification which is *useful* related information, but is not *central* (*core*) to the implementation, nor is it commentary.

children.name: Basis
children.definition: A basis is an underlying idea that is a foundation for a specification.

children.name: Claim
children.definition: 'Claim' is an assertion by a defined source, about a system attribute or an event. The Claim parameter is used to emphasize that the credibility of the claim is not high, and the reader should exercise their judgement and caution, because there is a risk that the claim might not

children.name: Common Causes
children.definition:
These are repetitive systemic causes of consistent measurable process output levels of performance or cost.
"Common causes: of variation, produce points on a control chart that over a long period all fall inside the control limits. Common causes of variation stay the same day to

children.name: Credibility Rating
children.definition: A credibility rating is the assignment of a number on a defined credibility scale that ranges from 0.0 (no credibility for an impact estimate) to 1.0 (perfect credibility of an impact estimate).

children.name: Credibility
children.definition:
Credibility expresses the strength of 'belief in' and hence 'validity of', information.
Within Impact Estimation, credibility is usually assessed for the *evidence* and *sources* supporting each specific impact estimate. Credibility is expressed as a numeric value, on a range fro

children.name: Critical Factor
children.definition:
A Critical Factor is an attribute level or condition in a system which can, on its own, determine the success or failure of the system under specified conditions.
A critical *failure* factor is usually specified as a constraint level (for example a 'Fail' or 'Survival' level), or

children.name: Evidence
children.definition:
Evidence is the historic facts which support an assertion. The evidence usually will have been the basis for making an assertion.
In Impact Estimation, evidence is required for each impact estimate. Where there is no evidence, it should be clearly stated that there is none.
**Key

children.name: False
children.definition: Predefined State. Same as Off.

children.name: Rationale
children.definition:
A rationale is the reasoning or principle that explains and thus seeks to justify a specification.
'Rationale' is a parameter for declaring information that justifies a specification.

children.name: Subjective
children.definition: **Subjective**: dependent on defined stakeholder value judgment. Not 'Objective'.

children.name: Agile
children.definition: Any set of tactics that enable a prioritized stream of useful results, in spite of a changing environment.

children.name: Plan
children.definition: **Plan [PDSA]** is the first phase of the Plan Do Study Act Cycle (*168). It involves specifying a theory or hypothesis — including a procedure for testing it — before any change is made to the process under improvement.

children.name: Waterfall Method
children.definition: The analogy in the term **Waterfall Method** refers to a series of waterfall stages as the 'water' (project progress) flows downstream.

children.name: Delivery Cycle
children.definition: A delivery cycle contains the initial operational implementation of an Evo Step, and its handover to stakeholders. A delivery cycle is a subset of a Result Cycle. A delivery cycle involves implementation activities such as training, installation and field-testing.

children.name: Deployment
children.definition: 'Deployment' means *actually delivering* an Evo step to a set of stakeholders. Deployment is the last stage of a Delivery Cycle.

children.name: Development Cycle
children.definition: A development cycle is an optional backroom cycle, within the result cycle of Evo. It is concerned with acquiring/purchasing and developing, any products required for the production and/or delivery cycles.

children.name: Do [PDSA]
children.definition: Do [PDSA] is part of the 'Plan Do Study Act' Cycle (See Plan Do Study Act Cycle *168). It involves implementing (Do…ing) what you have planned, that is, carrying out the 'experiment' to see how your plan measures up to reality.

children.name: Evolutionary
children.definition: The 'evolutionary' concept implies association with Evolutionary Project Management; an iterative process of change, feedback, learning and consequent change. Evolutionary processes need to be carefully distinguished from other processes — those that do not iterate, do not learn

children.name: Implementation Cycle
children.definition: An **implementation cycle** is part of a result cycle. It consists of the (Evo) development cycle, production cycle and delivery cycle. Implementation means 'taking a plan, or an idea, and turning it into reality'.

children.name: Incremental Development
children.definition: Incremental development means designing a system largely up-front, and then dividing its construction, and perhaps handover, into a series of cumulative increments.

children.name: Integration
children.definition: Integration is the process of inserting Evo step components into a system. It is part of the production cycle (which is one of the three major sub-processes for implementation of an Evo step: development, production, and delivery). Integration works with developed or acquired ste

children.name: Plan Do Study Act Cycle
children.definition: The **Plan Do Study Act Cycle** (PDSA Cycle) is a process cycle — a method for changing a defined work process so that it measurably improves. The cycle requires standardizing and stabilizing the target process first, so that the effects of any change can be credibly observed. De

children.name: Pre-requisite Steps
children.definition: **Pre-requisite Steps** are evolutionary steps that are defined as pre-requisite by some Planguage mechanism. Examples of mechanisms are use of parameters Starts, Before, During, Ends, After.

children.name: Production Cycle
children.definition: An optional backroom cycle, within the result cycle of Evo, concerned with product integration, or manufacturing and distribution of any products required for the delivery cycle.

children.name: Result Cycle
children.definition: Within Evo, a **Result Cycle** is an entire Evo step cycle aimed at delivering a result that moves towards satisfying the overall requirements. A result cycle consists of Plan Do Study Act (PDSA) activities.

children.name: Serial Development
children.definition: **Serial development** is a development process in which work proceeds on only one Evo Step at any one time — each step completes before the next begins.

children.name: Study [PDSA]
children.definition: **Study [PDSA]** is the third phase of the Plan-Do-Study-Act Cycle (*168). The Study phase observes and gathers data concerning the results of the Do phase.

children.name: Editor Advice Log
children.definition:
An Editor Advice Log is written formally by a scribe at an SQC Specification Meeting. It is based on oral reports from checkers.
**Contents:** issues · improvement suggestions · questions of intent for the specification writer.
**Writing mode:** brainstorming — volume now, analys

children.name: Template
children.definition: A **Template** is an example or 'model' of something, which can be used to help people to tailor or make something, based on that model.

children.name: Function, To
children.definition: 'To **function**' means to carry out the defined functions of a system under the defined conditions, at least at survival level or better, for performance and cost.

children.name: Function (adjective)
children.definition: A **function adjective** is used to restrict the modified noun (constraint as in function constraint) to the function area.

children.name: StatusToGoal
children.definition: **StatusToGoal** is the numeric gap between the current [[Now.513|Status *513]] and the [[Goal.109|Goal *109]] level. It measures how far the current performance is from the committed success target — the threshold at which success is declared and no further improvement priority

children.name: StatusToTolerable
children.definition: **StatusToTolerable** is the numeric gap between the current [[Now.513|Status *513]] and the [[Tolerable.539|Tolerable *539]] threshold. It measures how far the current performance is from the project-viability line — the boundary below which the whole project fails.

children.name: Attack
children.definition: Attacks are [[Threat.671|Threats]] activated. They attempt to cause negative consequences in a system.

children.name: Risk
children.definition: A Risk is the **possibility** of [[Damage.673|Damage]] occurring.

children.name: Threat
children.definition: A **threat** is something that can potentially cause some degree of project failure, lack of success or negative consequences.

children.name: Abbreviation
children.definition: A Planguage parameter meaning 'abbreviation'.

children.name: Class
children.definition: A class is a defined qualifier term category.

children.name: Numeric Tag
children.definition:
A term beginning with the 'asterisk *' sign, and immediately followed by a number. The Numeric Tag is the human-language-neutral unique tag for each Planguage Glossary-defined term.
**Rationale:** This *Tag is intended to help identify Planguage concepts unambiguously regardless

children.name: Tag
children.definition: A **Tag** is a term that serves to identify a statement, or set of statements, unambiguously.

children.name: Type
children.definition: **Type** specifies the category of a Planguage concept.

children.name: Variant
children.definition: A **variant** is a special variation of a Planguage artifact {handbook, slides, etc.}.

children.name: Version
children.definition: A **version** is an initial or changed specification instance.

children.name: XREF
children.definition: A Planguage-defined abbreviation meaning 'cross reference'.

children.name: Estimate, To
children.definition:
In Planguage, 'to estimate' is the process of arriving at a judgement, by guessing the probable numeric value, of a numeric attribute level, using other methods than immediate measurement. Estimation is not to be confused with Quantification or Measurement.
Webster's: "to judge o

children.name: Implementation
children.definition: An implementation is the real-life representation of an idea.

children.name: Process Improvement Suggestion
children.definition: A process improvement suggestion is an idea to change a process, in order to improve its performance and/or cost. Suggestions should be directed to the relevant process owner for evaluation (to see if they have sufficient value-to-cost impact).

children.name: Question of Intent
children.definition: A **Question of Intent** is a question concerning the technical intention of a Specification, directed to a Specification Writer. It is asked orally during the SQC Specification Meeting. It is immediately logged in the Editor Advice Log by the Scribe. It is answered orally by the

children.name: Chunk
children.definition: A 'chunk' is a portion of a document being evaluated by SQC, where the intent is to continue checking other chunks after the first chunk is checked, unless the defect data from a chunk is extreme ('too many' or 'zero' defects).

children.name: Commentary
children.definition: Commentary specifications are remarks about other specifications. Commentary specifications will probably not have any economic, quality or effort consequences if they are incorrect: defects in commentary are almost always of minor severity.

children.name: Evaluation Effort
children.definition:
This is the cost (in work hours) of determining the quality level (Remaining major defects per page) of a specification.
The process to do the evaluation is assumed to be SQC, but other processes to determine the quality level could be used. Use of sampling will dramatically redu

children.name: Item
children.definition: An item is a term for whatever gets reported by checkers and then logged by a Scribe during SQC logging.

children.name: Logical Page
children.definition: A logical page is defined as a defined number of *non-background* words. Default Logical Page volume: If no other definition is given, use '300 non-background words' per logical page as default.

children.name: Readership
children.definition: The readership (or intended readership) of a specification is all the 'types of people' we intend shall read or use the specification.

children.name: Review Focus
children.definition: A **Specification Review Focus** is the primary purpose of a review. It is in practice defined by the set of rules, checklists, process description, people participation, or other devices for analysing particular aspects of a specification. If the Spec QC process is used, then th

children.name: Sample
children.definition: In a quality control process, a **Sample** is a small part of a document, product or system, which is selected for checking. The intent of an SQC sample is that it will give *some* information about the specification without the *cost* of checking more of it — never to identify o

children.name: Dialect
children.definition: A 'Dialect' is a local variation in Planguage symbols or terminology due to local culture, habit, traditions or language variation.

children.name: Language
children.definition: An {agreed, understood, defined} {written, graphical or oral} means of expressing any ideas, concepts or notions. We are particularly interested in a specialised language for systems engineering and management, which we call "Planguage" here.

children.name: System Description Language
children.definition: **SDL** is the subset of Planguage for describing systems, including 'processes viewed as systems with attributes'.

children.name: Tailored Planguage
children.definition: **Tailored Planguage** is any modification to a defined version of Basic Planguage (*225) to tailor it to a specific environment.

children.name: Terminology
children.definition: **Terminology** is the vocabulary of technical terms used and defined in Planguage, and in projects which make use of it.

children.name: Translation
children.definition: A **translation** is a translation from (usually US English, the default language) a Planguage document to another major human language. Note: Planguage to UK English would be a dialect 'tuning' not a translation.

children.name: Actual Step Content
children.definition: The design ideas, modified by [actual qualifiers] and functionality modified by [actual qualifiers], which are actually delivered in a specific [[Evo-Step.141|Evo step]].

children.name: Innovation
children.definition: Order of magnitude, or better, improvement in performance/cost efficiency, in stakeholder-valued system attributes.

children.name: Life Cycle
children.definition: The life cycle is the entire duration of existence of a defined system — from inception to retirement or disposal, independently of the specific methods used for development and maintenance.

children.name: Plan
children.definition: A **Plan** (*108) is an idea, or more likely a set of ideas, created with a view to possible future implementation.

children.name: Time Between Successive Products
children.definition: The **TBSP** is calculated by subtracting the release date of the earlier product from that of the later product, giving calendar days difference.

children.name: Acquisition
children.definition: Acquisition is the activity of obtaining a [[Component.022|component]]. Acquisition is part of the [[Development-Cycle.413|Development Cycle]].

children.name: Act
children.definition: Act [PDSA] is part of the [[Plan-Do-Study-Act-Cycle.168|Plan-Do-Study-Act Cycle]]. The 'Act' phase decides on what course of action should be taken based on the information supplied by the 'Study' phase. It is to standardize the process at a new level, to draw new conclusions abo

children.name: Act
children.definition: An 'act' is a process of doing something, by means of humans or other Agents.

children.name: Entry Condition
children.definition: An entry condition is a written part of a work-process standard. Entry conditions are usually found in sets. The relevant set of entry conditions is evaluated in an entry process. They are used to determine if there is entry permission to a task process.

children.name: Entry Process
children.definition: An entry process involves evaluating any applicable entry conditions for a process. The process itself is defined by a main task. When *all* entry conditions are met, the main process task may officially commence.

children.name: Exit Condition
children.definition: An exit condition is a written part of a work-process standard. Exit conditions are usually found in sets. The relevant set of exit conditions is evaluated in an exit process. They are used to determine if there is exit permission from a task process. All the generic and specific

children.name: Exit Process
children.definition:
An exit process involves evaluating any applicable exit conditions for a process. Only when *all* exit conditions are met, can the main process task officially terminate and any process output be released to the next process.
*Note:* If any conditions fail, the exit process inclu

children.name: Parallel Development
children.definition: **Parallel Development** is any development of more than one Evo step that takes place at the same time.

children.name: Planning
children.definition: **Planning** (*382) is a human activity of 'visualizing the future,' with the intents of being prepared for it and modifying future States to suit Stakeholder purposes. Its scope includes analysis, requirement specification, design, design analysis, quality control, and project m

children.name: Platform Development
children.definition: A product development process based on products derived from a common cohesive, underlying architecture, and related synchronized development processes and organizational values [JANDOUREK96 (HP)]. **Platform Development** is an attempt to reuse 10% to 90% of the common elements

children.name: Project
children.definition: A project is an activity to produce change to a defined system.

children.name: Strategic Management Cycle
children.definition: A **strategic management cycle** is a cycle within a result cycle concerned with controlling and monitoring the overall change process. It approves proposed changes against strategic objectives and adopted high-level strategies, co-ordinates with other programs and projects, acqu

children.name: Sub-Process
children.definition: A **sub-process** is a process contained in a supra-process.

children.name: Supra-process
children.definition: A process that contains other defined processes.

children.name: Task
children.definition: A **Task** is a defined and limited piece of work.

children.name: Trade
children.definition: **Trade** is a type of activity done by groups. E.g. 'The computer trade.'

children.name: Work Process
children.definition: A **Work Process** is a defined process for carrying out human work.

children.name: Adaptive
children.definition: 'Adaptive' refers to the set of concepts which are interesting in relation to changing a system from one defined state to another. This can be while a system is in operation (user changes operational parameters). It can refer to system modification such as porting, extending, imp

children.name: Cost
children.definition: 'Cost' as an adjective is used to signify that *Resources*, rather than *Qualities*, *Functions*, or *Designs*, are the category of the noun being used.

children.name: Generic
children.definition: Generic means *applicable to any individual component* of a group of components within a defined scope. Generic means general, as opposed to specific. 'Generic' things are often 'reusable' (with local tailoring that makes them more specific) in a variety of situations.

children.name: Add
children.definition: Add is a Planguage verb indicating the addition of some specification to a defined set of specifications.

children.name: Combine
children.definition: Combine means: to put together, in some sense and manner.

children.name: Component
children.definition: A component is a potential, or actual, part of some larger system, or specification.

children.name: Consists of
children.definition: Parameter: Describes the *complete* set of elements that a concept consists of.

children.name: Except
children.definition: 'Except' is a parameter which means that the following term or expression is an exception from the previous term or expression.

children.name: Explosion
children.definition: Explosion is a 'dramatic' word for 'hierarchical decomposition of complex specifications into useful, more elementary, detail'.

children.name: Includes
children.definition: 'Includes' expresses the concept of inclusion of a set of components within a larger set of components. 'A Includes B.' means that B is a sub-component of the component A.

children.name: Is Part Of
children.keyedIcon: X {y}.    meaning y Is Part Of X
children.definition: A Parameter which indicates that a specification is a component or element of something else.

children.name: Remove
children.keyedIcon: -' in context referring to a defined set of specs
children.definition: Remove is a Planguage verb indicating the removal of some specification from a defined set of specifications.

children.name: Replace
children.definition: Replace is a Planguage verb indicating the replacement of some specification with another.

children.name: Set
children.definition: A **set** is a list of terms that belong together in some defined sense — a named collection of related items, expressed using curly-brace notation `{ }` in Planguage.

children.name: Structure
children.definition: A **structure** is the observable implementation of a system component — the way it is built.

children.name: Subset
children.definition: A **Subset** is a specified, or defined, part of a specified, or defined, larger whole.

children.name: Measure of Effectiveness
children.definition: A **Measure of Effectiveness** is the quantified impact of a defined Measure of Performance (*482, MoP) on a defined system under defined environmental conditions.

children.name: Meter
children.definition: A **Meter** parameter is used to identify, or specify, the definition of a practical measuring device, process, or test that has been selected for use in measuring a numeric value (level) on a defined Scale. *(Keyed icon: `-|?|-` — a `?` on top of the Scale icon `-|-|-`.)*

children.name: Metric
children.keyedIcon: -|-|-> (Scale with units) or ---> (Scalar Arrow, simplified without explicit units)
children.definition: A **Metric** is a system of related measures that facilitates the quantification of an attribute. The metric may be composed of one or more measure dimensions or characteristics. A *complex* attribute specification — one defined with a set of several Scales of Measure — is *also*

children.name: Process Output Metrics
children.definition: Measures of attributes of a specific process 'output' (see process output attributes).

children.name: And
children.definition: 'And' is used as a logical operator to join any two expressions within a statement.

children.name: If
children.definition: **If** is a logical operator parameter used in qualifiers to explicitly specify conditions. The `If` is *implied* for all terms in a qualifier — however, `If` may be used to communicate a condition more explicitly to the novice reader. The keyed icon `?` may be used before a cond

children.name: Or
children.definition: **Or** is a logical operator used in qualifiers, or other appropriate specifications, to indicate alternative conditions. If any one **Or** condition is true, then the set of conditions is true.

children.name: Planguage Parameter
children.definition: Planguage Parameter is the taxonomy class for all Planguage keywords used in specifications (Goal, Fail, Meter, Source, Risk, etc.). It is a grouping concept: every Planguage keyword is a kind of Planguage Parameter, organised into 14 sub-groups (Identification, Description, Scop

children.name: Pointer
children.definition: A **Pointer** is a stable symbolic reference to a potentially evolving definition. There are several types of references (informally, "pointers") in Planguage: Tags (character strings that name a parameter or specification), Sources (references to the origin of a specification),

children.name: Complex
children.definition: Compound in structure; consisting of interconnected parts.

children.name: Complicated
children.definition: Anything, that is difficult to understand, estimate or predict the actions, reactions, and attributes of.

children.name: Compound
children.definition: Compound entities contain two or more elements.

children.name: Downstream
children.keyedIcon: <~  (A <~ B means A is downstream of B)
children.definition:
Relative to a given process, 'downstream' refers to any processes which are carried out later, and implies that they are impacted in some way by that upstream process.
**Usage:** 'Customer use' is downstream from 'pilot testing'.
**Parameter:** Downstream. Long form = Downstream

children.name: Elementary
children.definition:
An 'elementary' component is not decomposed into sub-components.
A component can be elementary because it is unable to be decomposed into sub-components, or because there is no declared intent to decompose it.

children.name: Hierarchical
children.definition: Hierarchical is an adjective used to describe 'belonging to a hierarchy'. The elements of a hierarchy can be organized by some classification into distinct levels, where there is a relationship between the levels. Either the higher levels have some kind of authority or control ov

children.name: Local
children.definition: 'Local' is an adjective used to specify that something applies only to a restricted subset of a defined scope.

children.name: Lower Level
children.definition: Something lower in a hierarchy than high-levels.

children.name: Goal
children.definition: A Goal is a primary numeric target level of performance.

children.name: Stretch
children.definition: A **Stretch** parameter is used to define a somewhat more ambitious target level than the committed Goal or Budget levels.

children.name: Wish
children.definition: A **Wish** parameter is used to specify a stakeholder-valued, not-committed target level for a scalar attribute.

children.name: Aspect, in [ASPECT] book 2026
children.definition: Any distinguishable property, perspective, or dimension used to describe, analyze, or evaluate an entity.

children.name: Impact
children.definition: An **impact** is the estimated or actual numeric effect of a design idea (or set of design ideas or Evo step) on a requirement attribute under given conditions. Full impact information includes: a scale impact, a percentage impact, and uncertainty data (known error margins). The

children.name: Impacts
children.definition: The **Impacts** parameter is used to identify the set of attributes that are considered likely to be impacted by a given attribute (usually another requirement attribute or a proposed design idea).

children.name: Specification Element
children.definition: A **Specification Element** is any distinct element, however elementary or complex, of a specification. A specification element can be a statement, an expression, or a term.

children.name: Defect Prevention Process
children.definition: The **Defect Prevention Process (DPP)** is a specific IBM-originated process of continuous process improvement. It is part of Specification Quality Control (SQC).

children.name: Design Process
children.definition:
The design process is the act of searching for, specifying, evaluating and selecting design ideas, in an attempt to satisfy specified stakeholder requirements.
Design is finding a set of solutions (design ideas) for a set of defined requirements.

children.name: Evolutionary Project Management
children.definition:
A project management process delivering 'high-value-first' progress towards the *currently defined and approved requirements*, and then seeking to obtain, and use, realistic, early feedback.
Key components include: frequent delivery of system changes (steps); steps delivered to s

children.name: Illuminate
children.definition: (verb) A process that provides increased understanding of a concept, for a set of defined and purposeful conditions. To create Illumination (*833).

children.name: Impact Estimation
children.definition: **Impact Estimation** is a Planguage method/process to evaluate the quantitative impacts of design ideas on requirements.

children.name: Requirements Process
children.definition:
The requirements process includes all aspects of requirements gathering and maintenance, including but not limited to:
- requirements solicitation (including stakeholder analysis)
- requirements analysis
- requirements quality control
- requirements review
- requirements change m

children.name: Action
children.definition: Action is a specification parameter which describes an action to be taken under defined circumstances.

children.name: Event
children.definition:
An event is a specified occurrence.
An event must be clearly distinguishable from the non-occurrence of the event. It must be reliably observable, testable, or measurable in the real world. Consequently, events must be precisely defined — unambiguously. An event usually results i

children.name: Evo Step Specification
children.definition:
An Evo step specification is the formal written definition of the content of an Evo step.
An Evo step specification can differ from the reality of the delivered step content.

children.name: Evo Step
children.definition:
An Evo step ('evolutionary step' or, simply 'step') is a 'package of change', containing a set of design ideas, that on delivery to a system, is intended to help move the system towards meeting the yet-unfulfilled system requirements.
Evo steps are assumed to be small increments,

children.name: Input
children.definition: Input (or System Input) is anything which enters a system.

children.name: Mega-step
children.definition: A **Mega-step** is an evolutionary 'step', or step plan, which includes two or more delivery steps.

children.name: Output
children.definition: An **output** (or system output) is the result of a system.

children.name: Process Input
children.definition: A process input is any data and/or materials input into a process.

children.name: Process Output
children.definition: A process output is any data or materials output from a process.

children.name: Step Element
children.definition: A **step element** is any component of a step specification. In practice this can be one or more of: a design idea (including strategies, architecture, solutions); a function requirement; a step specification defined elsewhere but reused in a new qualifier context (e.g., Step-ABC

children.name: Step Task
children.definition: A **step task** is any component of an Evo delivery step that has to be carried out in order to deliver the planned impact, but is not itself a specific design idea or function (step content) to be delivered to the host system. Step tasks are the process overhead components of a

children.name: Method
children.definition: A **Method** is a body of systematic techniques used by a specific discipline.

children.name: Process
children.definition: A process is the set of Entry Process, Task and Exit Process. A process is formally defined or definable. All formal processes contain tasks. A task alone is not a formal defined process.

children.name: Debugging
children.definition: A process of removing identified faults (bugs) from a system. The process should include fault-consequent revalidation (regression testing) confirming that the fault removal succeeded and has not inadvertently injected additional faults.

children.name: Logging
children.definition: 'Logging' is the writing of notes (logs) according to defined standards with the intention of their later use.

children.name: Quality Control
children.definition: **Quality Control (QC)** is the generic name for a set of processes that try to check the quality of a work product compared to applicable 'standards' — rules that define acceptable quality. QC includes testing, Specification Quality Control (SQC), and any other activity such as

children.name: Quantify, To
children.definition: To **quantify** is to specify numerically. To articulate a variable attribute, using a defined scale of measure, and specifying one or more benchmark or target levels on the Scale. The resulting specification is 'quantified'. In Planguage, quantification begins with the definitio

children.name: Statistical Process Control
children.definition: **Statistical Process Control (SPC)** is a method for analysis of statistical process data that aims to improve performance levels and reduce the variability of results. Emphasis is placed on distinguishing between systemic problems — which can only be cured by changing the syste

children.name: Validation
children.definition: **Validation** is a process of confirming that a specification is complete and correct.

children.name: Verification
children.definition: A **verification** process tries to confirm that the output of a process corresponds to expectations.

children.name: Condition
children.definition: A condition is a specified pre-requisite for making a specification or a system component valid.

children.name: Generic Qualifier
children.definition: A Generic Qualifier is a set of higher level concepts, which are going to be decomposed into specific subsets and combinations, for use as qualifiers for any Planguage statement. Scale Qualifiers are a particular type (for Scale) of Generic Qualifiers.

children.name: Qualifier
children.definition: A **qualifier** is a defined set of conditions, embedded in or referenced by a specification. All of its conditions must be 'true' for that specification to apply. A qualifier defines any interesting set of specific time, location, and event conditions — sometimes classified as '

children.name: Illumination
children.definition: (noun) The degree to which a named object understands a defined artifact for a defined purpose.

children.name: Check, To
children.definition: To 'check' a specification means to determine if it is consistent with any applicable specification rules (standards), which it *should* be consistent with.

children.name: Checking
children.definition:
Checking is the name of a sub-process within Specification Quality Control (SQC).
'Checking' is also the name of a widespread SQC activity, ('checking' with a small 'c'), which although *predominantly* carried out within the Checking [SQC] sub-process, is also used to some degree

children.name: Defect Detection Process
children.definition: The **Defect Detection Process (DDP)** is part of Specification Quality Control (SQC), which also includes the Defect Prevention Process (DPP). It is the systematic, project-focussed process of identifying and fixing specification defects.

children.name: Edit Audit [SQC]
children.definition:
Edit Audit is an SQC sub-process, carried out by a team leader, to verify that reasonable and complete editing has been done.
**Note:** Edit Audit will try to make sure that valid main specification rules, the editor advice log, relevant editing and specification procedures, and

children.name: Edit [SQC]
children.definition: The Edit sub-process of SQC primarily attempts to correct a specification by removing identified defects. The Edit process includes any defined Edit process activity, such as sending messages to other specification owners about possible problems with their specification.

children.name: Exit [SQC]
children.definition: Exit is the name of an SQC sub-process. The SQC team leader checks a set of defined SQC exit conditions, and decides whether to allow the specification to exit, based on the exit condition status; or whether to take other action, as a result of unsatisfied exit conditions.

children.name: Quality Assurance
children.definition: **Quality Assurance (QA)** is the generic name for any set of activities which have as their primary or partial intent, or effect, to influence ('assure') the quality levels of a product or process. QA includes but is not limited to Quality Control — it also encompasses quality s

children.name: Test
children.definition: To **test** is to plan and execute an analytical process on any system, product or process, where we attempt to understand if the system performs as expected, or not.

children.name: Efficiency (noun adjective)
children.definition: The noun adjective 'Efficiency' can be used to refer to any set of Performance to Cost Attribute ratios. For example: 'Efficiency Attributes, Efficiency Requirements, Efficiency Benchmarks, Efficiency Targets, and Efficiency Records.'

children.name: Performance
children.definition: System performance is an attribute set that describes measurably 'how good' the system is at delivering *effectiveness* to its stakeholders. Each individual performance attribute level has a different 'effectiveness,' for different stakeholders, and consequently different value o

children.name: Quality
children.definition: A **quality** is a scalar attribute reflecting 'how well' a system functions as viewed by a defined Stakeholder. Quality includes: {Availability, Usability, Integrity, Adaptability, and many others}. All qualities can be described numerically using a defined Scale, or set of Scal

children.name: Simplicity
children.definition: **Simplicity** is a numeric level, stated on a defined Scale of Measure, for defined conditions, including Who, How, Where and When.

children.name: Scalar
children.definition: A **Scalar** is an adjective used to describe objects that possess or are measured using at least one scale of measure. Numeric levels on a scale of measure are described as *scalar* values, contrasting with binary objects that exist only in one of two discrete states.

children.name: Baseline To Target Pair
children.definition: In [[Impact-Estimation.283|Impact Estimation]], this is a set of two numeric values associated with a specific requirement under stated conditions: the Scale value for the benchmark reference point (0%) and the Scale value for the target (100%).

children.name: Constraint Attribute Impact
children.definition: An acknowledgement, probably by conscious analysis and explicit specification — and perhaps by quantitative estimation of the degree — that a specific [[Constraint-Attribute.687|Constraint Attribute]] has an impact on one or more system objects or sets of objects of interest.

children.name: Control Axis
children.definition: The Process Control Axis is the horizontal, left-to-right direction of 'process flow' in a Planguage process diagram.

children.name: Deviation
children.definition: Deviation is the amount (estimated or actual) by which some attribute differs from some specific benchmark or target. Deviation is usually expressed numerically using either absolute or percentage difference.

children.name: Effect
children.keyedIcon: any benchmark or generic level of performance, e.g. O----|----> or O-----<-----<<----->
children.definition:
The result ('the effect') of using a system performance attribute (the 'cause').
Formally: the differential value to a defined stakeholder, caused by a defined level of a defined system attribute, acting on a defined stakeholder, in a defined stakeholder environment.
More simply

children.name: Effectiveness
children.definition:
**Effectiveness** is a measure of how good the current attributes of a system are at delivering the stakeholders' current demands of the system.
Effectiveness is a raw measure of impact, and does not contain information about the costs of making that impact (performance *in relat

children.name: Efficiency
children.definition:
**Efficiency** is 'effectiveness' in relation to cost.
A benefit to cost ratio or a performance to cost ratio would be a measure of efficiency.

children.name: Impact Estimate
children.definition: An **impact estimate** is an evaluated guess as to the result of implementing a design idea.
