In other words, it is a considered, quantified guess of the effect on a specific scalar requirement attribute (performance or resource) of implementing a design idea (or set of design ide

children.name: Meter
children.definition: A **Meter** (noun) is anything defined with the Meter parameter (*093). It is the concrete artefact — a measurement device, test process, or counting procedure — that results from writing a `Meter:` specification block.

children.name: Performance to Cost Ratio
children.definition: For a design idea (or set of design ideas or an Evo step), the ratio of the performance improvements to the cost of the resources needed to implement them. For a selected set of requirements: **Performance to Cost Ratio = Sum of Performance / Sum of Costs**. Such ratios allow com

children.name: Precision
children.definition: Precision is a general specification quality. It is the degree to which a specification points out exactly and accurately the system components (e.g. stakeholders, design functions, sub-systems) for which the specification is *intended* by the Author to apply. And consequently, i

children.name: Resolution
children.definition: The solution of a problem is a resolution.

children.name: Sum for Requirement
children.definition: A **Sum for Requirement** is, for a given set of design ideas, the sum of their estimated or measured percentage impacts on a single performance or resource attribute.

children.name: Sum of Costs
children.definition: Within an Impact Estimation table, for a specific design idea (or set of design ideas or Evo step), the **Sum of Costs** is the vertical sum of the percentage impacts of selected scalar resource attributes.

children.name: Sum of Performance
children.definition: Within an Impact Estimation table, the **Sum of Performance** is the total quantitative impact on the specified performance targets made by a specific design idea (or set of design ideas or Evo step).

children.name: Uncertainty
children.definition: **Uncertainty** is the degree to which we are in doubt about how an impact estimate, or measurement, of an attribute reflects reality.

children.name: Value Chain
children.definition: A **value chain** is a sequence of two or more defined objects. The initial object produces value, as defined by the second object's value.

children.name: Value To Cost Ratio
children.definition: The **value to cost ratio** is a numeric expression of perceived stakeholder value to estimated or actual costs, for a set of design ideas or for an Evo step.

children.name: Value to Cost Score
children.definition: The **value to cost score** is a simple numeric scoring mechanism, sometimes used in meetings to share opinions, and to arrive at a consensus about the value and cost of Evo steps. The scale is 0 to 9, where 9 is the score representing highest value, or highest cost.

children.name: Acceptable Level
children.definition: Any numeric level in the [[Acceptable-Range.545|acceptable range]].

children.name: Tolerable Range
children.definition: The **Tolerable Range** is the band on a scalar attribute axis where the project is alive — at or above the [[Tolerable.539|Tolerable]] threshold — but below the committed success level ([[Goal.109|Goal]]). The project is not failing, but it has not yet reached its target.

children.name: Landing Zone
children.definition: A landing zone is a target range that stretches from just better than a Fail level through the Goal/Budget level to the Stretch Level.

children.name: Level
children.definition: A level is a defined numeric position on a scale of measure.

children.name: Limit
children.definition: A limit is a numeric level at a border — that is, at an edge of a scalar range (a success range, an acceptable range, a failure range, or a catastrophe range). It is specifically used at the edges of ranges associated with constraints: the fail limit and the survival limit / cata

children.name: Locus
children.definition: A 'locus' is the integration of all factors/elements that define a scalar level. A locus consists of: a specified scalar level; a specified unit of measure; a units of measure context. The objective of all additional information is to improve the clarity and reality of the specif

children.name: Or Better
children.definition: **Or Better** is an expression used within a scalar specification to explicitly emphasise that the specified level has a range of acceptable values, rather than being just a fixed, single value. In other words, **Or Better** helps identify the specified level as the beginning of

children.name: Or Worse
children.definition: **Or Worse** is an expression used within a scale specification to explicitly emphasise that the specified level has a range of unacceptable values, rather than being just a fixed, single value. In other words, **Or Worse** helps identify the beginning of a 'no go' range.

children.name: Priority Level
children.definition: **Priority Level** refers to the specified attribute level class {Wish, Stretch, Goal, Fail, Survival}. The final priority relationship is determined by other factors such as qualifier and Authority. Priority Level *471 is the parameter used to describe the attribute level's rela

children.name: Range
children.definition: A **range** is the extent between and including two defined numeric levels on a scale of measure. Range, as used in the figure, captures a snapshot of some common scalar attribute ranges using the target and constraint levels. Examples of different range classifications include:

children.name: Step Level
children.definition: A **step level** specification is a sub-class of a Goal level. A Step Level is intended for specification of intermediate scalar levels of both performance and resources, where these levels are not primary product or system targets in themselves — they are approximate plans for e

children.name: Until
children.definition: **Until** is a logical operator that is used to limit the extent of a scalar range of values.

children.name: Commonality
children.definition: If any two products share any common assets they have commonality.

children.name: Dependency
children.definition: A 'dependency' is a reliance of some kind, of one set of components on another set of components. Any given component can be part of numerous dependencies (either having one or more dependencies, and/or having one or more dependencies placed on it). The parameter 'Dependency,' or

children.name: Impacted By
children.definition: **Impacted By** is used to indicate any *other* specified items, (such as requirements, objectives, designs, policies, or conditions), which affect, or might affect, a defined specification itself, or what it refers to.

children.name: Inherited
children.definition: A specification element is termed 'inherited' if it applies *implicitly* to a specific specification. Inherited specification elements are not *directly* specified in a statement (that is, they are not local to a given specification), but they are inherited from related specifica

children.name: Kin
children.definition: Kin specifications are specifications which derive from an identical set of source specifications. For example, test plans, source code and user handbooks could all be derived from the same requirements or the same design.

children.name: Parallelity
children.definition: **Parallelity** is having a number of parallel Evolutionary cycles. These can be any type of Evo cycles — frontroom or backroom (concurrent engineering).

children.name: Parent
children.definition: A parent is the *immediate superior* component to a kid.

children.name: Relationship
children.definition:
A relationship is a connection between objects.
For example, A |-| B. "A is in a relationship to B. There is no notion of impact — just connectedness."

children.name: Sibling
children.definition: A **sibling** is a "parallel kid" — a specification artifact (process, function, system, delivery step, or other entity) that shares the same parent as another artifact at the same level of derivation.

children.name: Support System
children.definition: A **Support System** is any system that has performance levels that impact a defined stakeholder environment. A Support System is intended to contribute to the stakeholder benefit level.

children.name: Supported By
children.definition: **Supported By** is used to list the tags of any and all specifications that contribute usefully to the accomplishment of a defined requirement.

children.name: Supports
children.definition: **Supports** is used to indicate what an attribute is mainly intended to support.

children.name: Supra
children.definition: 'Supra-' is a prefix, which can be attached to any component type that has its own sub-components (kids).

children.name: Upstream
children.definition: **Upstream** refers to any earlier processes than the one currently identified (the current reference point).

children.name: Cause-Effect Level
children.definition: A Cause-Effect Level is a layer in HumanAgent Gilb's Value Delivery hierarchy where causes at one level produce effects at the next level. Five levels stack: Business -> Stakeholder -> Product -> Solution -> Evo. Effects at lower levels become causes for the level above; this cha

children.name: Change Requirement
children.definition: A 'change requirement' represents a 'differential' change with reference to a defined 'baseline' system.

children.name: Commitment Parameters
children.definition: Future requirements specification levels which are 'promised' at some level.

children.name: Constraint
children.definition:
A constraint is a requirement that explicitly and intentionally tries to directly restrict any system or process.
A key property of a constraint is that a **penalty or loss** of some kind applies if the constraint is not respected.
Constraints include limitations on the engineeri

children.name: Core Purpose
children.definition: A Core Purpose is the most fundamental 'why?' the organisation exists. It can be viewed as the most fundamental *objective*; the most fundamental *measure* of progress or improvement; the measure that all supporting strategies intend to improve. We must always aim to improve in t

children.name: Critical Failure Factor
children.definition:
A Critical Failure Factor is any factor that determines any degree of failure of a system. This includes, and can be specified and articulated using, both scalar levels and binary conditions.
A critical failure factor may be specified as a constraint level (for example a 'Fail' o

children.name: Critical Success Factor
children.definition: Any attribute level or condition of a system that can itself, *alone or in combination with other factors*, determine practical or total system success, is a Critical Success Factor.

children.name: End
children.definition:
Future requirement or objective. Desired end state.
Generic synonym for *100.Objective.

children.name: Function Requirement
children.keyedIcon: (Function Tag) — parentheses symbolise the oval icon; alternative O.@
children.definition:
A **function requirement** specifies that the presence or absence of a defined function is required.
A function requirement is binary, and can either be a specific function target or a generic function constraint.

children.name: Function Target
children.definition:
A **function target** is a specific qualified function requirement type.
A function target is a specific testable function; it is not generic, nor is it a function constraint.

children.name: Generic Requirement
children.definition: A generic requirement is one intended for potential use in many systems or sub-systems. It is always reusable, and often tailorable.

children.name: Means Objective
children.definition: **Means objectives** are a 'strategy', in the format of a performance objective, to meet strategic objectives. They exist only to support meeting strategic objectives.

children.name: Mission
children.definition: A mission specifies who we are (or what we do) in relation to the rest of the world. It is the highest level of function of a system. The mission should not contain 'vision' description ('We make the best planes in the world'). It is an un-dramatic statement of the main function

children.name: Objective
children.definition:
Independent of a given set of values. Not 'Subjective'.
**Objective Quality:** Quantifiable quality levels independent of the value judgement (good or bad levels) of defined stakeholders. Example: "The mean time to repair an average fault is less than 24 hours."

children.name: Requirement Specification
children.definition: A requirement specification is a defined set of requirements. It also includes any relevant requirement background, such as benchmarks, and also any appropriate commentary.

children.name: Resource Budget
children.definition:
A resource budget describes how much of a resource we plan to have available.
A resource budget is a target level (Goal, Wish, Stretch) of a specified resource, which is related to a specific system component, with defined qualifiers for 'where', 'when' and 'events'. This implies

children.name: Scalar Target
children.definition: A **Scalar Target** is a performance target or resource target level specification expressed on a defined scale of measure. Scalar targets define stakeholder-valued levels of system performance and development costs, and are distinct from scalar constraints (like Fail) and benchm

children.name: Story: Stakeholder Story
children.definition: A **story** (§) is a very high-level definition of a requirement, containing just enough information so that: it can be made more structured and better clarified as a proper formal requirement if necessary; it enables a rough understanding of expected value, stakeholders involved

children.name: Measure, To
children.definition: To **measure** is to determine the numeric level of a scalar attribute under specified conditions, using a defined process, by means of examining a real system.

children.name: Requirements Engineering
children.definition:
Requirements Engineering is a requirements process carried out with an engineering level of rigor.
Requirements Engineering includes all aspects of requirements gathering and maintenance, including but not limited to:
- requirements solicitation (including stakeholder analysis)
-

children.name: Requirements Specification Process
children.definition: The process of specification of requirements.

children.name: Budget
children.definition: A 'budget' is an allocation of a limited resource.

children.name: Cost Budget
children.definition: A cost budget is a requirement level set for a resource. Cost budgets are either Budget Constraints or Budget Targets.

children.name: Cost Design
children.definition: Cost design is conscious design specification aimed at, or at least incidentally resulting in, the achievement of specified cost targets and cost constraints.

children.name: Cost-Level Constraint
children.definition: A cost-level constraint specifies a cost-level limitation on a defined resource scale. It is a numeric cost requirement constraint on the costs of design ideas, for a specified function or system.

children.name: Resource Constraint
children.definition:
A resource constraint is a resource requirement, which specifically *restricts*, or *serves as a warning* about, the level that can be used of a resource.
A resource constraint is specified as a scalar resource attribute level. It signals the level at which *some degree of system

children.name: Resource Requirement
children.definition:
A resource requirement specifies how much of a resource should be made available for later consumption.
A resource requirement is a scalar attribute with one or more resource targets and/or resource constraints specified.

children.name: Resource Saving Requirement
children.definition:
A resource saving requirement is a 'resource reduction' performance requirement. It specifies the specific savings in resource utilization that are needed: 'how much' is to be saved.
The focus is that it is the specific level of *saving* that is the requirement (as opposed to the

children.name: Resource Survival limit
children.definition: A Survival limit (*440) on a scalar resource use.

children.name: Resource Target
children.definition:
A resource target is a qualified resource level we aim, or might possibly aim, towards keeping within, while working towards performance goal levels.
Three parameters are used to specify resource targets {Budget, Stretch and Wish}. A Budget level is the *primary* resource target

children.name: Resource Type Constraint
children.definition: A **Resource Type Constraint** puts an explicit generic restriction on use of resource types or classes to solve a problem. It is a restriction (*498) and not itself a resource budget.

children.name: Resource Allocation
children.definition:
The total quantity of a defined resource which has been allocated for defined purposes, at defined times, under defined conditions.
This is not just any budget, but some larger allocation for a company, division, project or phase from which individual budgets specifications may b

children.name: Resource Assumption
children.definition:
A resource assumption is an estimate or guess about the total quantity of a defined resource which will be available under given conditions [when, where, if].
This is not the same as a specific resource allocation. But the assumption is a useful basis for deciding on the allocati

children.name: Resource Available
children.definition: The resource available is the remaining portion of the resource allocated that can be used to budget designs, tasks or Evo steps.

children.name: Resource Efficiency
children.definition:
Resource efficiency is a system attribute describing how well resources are utilized when the system produces output.
For a given system output level, better resource efficiency means 'using less resources'.

children.name: Resource Observation
children.definition: A resource observation is a determination, by any means, of the quantity of a defined resource that is available, at a given time, location and conditions.

children.name: Architecture Review
children.definition: An architecture review is a review process which looks at the *entire* set of engineering artifacts for a given system at a given level of process or development.

children.name: Clarity Review
children.definition:
A Clarity Review is a specification review which is primarily used to make sure the specification is clear enough to be interpreted correctly by the intended spec readership, as intended by the spec writers.
In particular, a clarity review is not initially concerned with the engi

children.name: Specification Content Review
children.definition: A **Specification Content Review (SCR)** is a class of specification review that focuses on the *goodness of the ideas* specified, regardless of *how well* they are specified. It asks: 'Is this the right stuff to do?' It looks at *content of concept* — not format or packaging — a

children.name: Specification Quality Control
children.definition: **Specification Quality Control (SQC)** is a rigorous specification quality control discipline concerned with defect detection, defect measurement, defect removal, process improvement, and entry/exit controls. It is based on evaluating specification conformance to specification r

children.name: Checker
children.definition:
A checker is a person, who performs checking within Specification Quality Control (SQC). It is a defined role in the process, and the checking activity can occur in most of the SQC sub-processes, not just the predominant 'checkers' process itself.
Checkers check specifications ag

children.name: Expert
children.definition:
A source that knows the state of the art levels in a defined discipline, and how to make them happen in practice.
*Note on 'Source':* 'Source' is used to include the idea that 'it does not matter if the expertise comes from a person, a group, or a written source such as a book, a

children.name: Facilitator
children.definition: A person or group who assists others in carrying out a work process, such as quality control or setting objectives; by virtue of their being especially trained, qualified, and knowledgeable in that process.

children.name: Participant
children.definition: A person or group who participates actively in a defined process.

children.name: Mitigation
children.definition: Mitigation is any Strategy which is intended to deal with a Threat (potential Attack), or an actual Attack, within the system, or by being added on after the Threat has successfully penetrated the system (Attack has occurred).

children.name: Safety Factor
children.keyedIcon: nX  (where n is the numeric safety factor)
children.definition: A **Safety Factor** is the dimensionless ratio of 'conscious over-design' that is either required, or actually applied to some part of a system. It communicates and prescribes the degree of deliberate margin built into a design beyond the minimum required level.

children.name: Safety Impact
children.definition: **Safety Impact** is the % deviation from target levels (targets = 0% level). It is an indirect measure of how well a required safety factor is met in theory or in practice. A positive safety impact for performance means the design exceeds the target; a positive safety impact for

children.name: Side Effect
children.definition: A **Side Effect** is an impact by a design idea on any requirement attribute, other than the direct impact(s) we primarily intended.

children.name: Survival
children.definition: Survival is a state where the system can exist. Outside the survival range is a 'dead' system caused by a specific attribute level being outside the survival range.

children.name: Stakeholder
children.keyedIcon: ←¶→  primary bilateral-exchange icon (2026-05-16, Tom Gilb): solid ← = value received · ¶ = identity (paragraph of interests + human profile facing left) · dashed → = resources given; :-|  neutral sentiment; :-)  satisfied; :-(  unhappy
children.definition: A **stakeholder** is any person, group, or object that has some direct or indirect interest in a *defined* system. Stakeholders can exercise control over both the immediate system operational characteristics and long-term system lifecycle considerations (such as portability, life

children.name: Design Content Rules
children.definition:
Design rules state expected design practices.
Design (content) rules give advice on best practices and recommended practices when designing (or architecting, or design engineering, or finding means or strategies). Deviation from Design Content Rules should be the basis for a desi

children.name: Specification Rule
children.definition: A **Specification Rule** focuses on the question: "Is the specification well written?" A set of specification rules states how we should both ensure and check such things as the completeness, unambiguousness, accuracy, and intelligibility of information in a specific type of spec

children.name: System Rules
children.definition: **System Rules** is the generic concept containing the sub-class business rules and specification rules.

children.name: Safety Deviation
children.definition: A **Safety Deviation** is a measure of the estimated-or-observed difference between a required safety margin, and the estimated or actual system attribute level. It answers: 'How safe is the current design?' or 'How safe are we compared to plan?'

children.name: Safety Margin
children.definition: A **Safety Margin** is a scalar difference between a required defined target or constraint level, and its calculated safety level derived using the appropriate safety factor. It expresses how much over-design is required, in the attribute's own units or as a percentage.

children.name: Status (Generic)
children.definition: A **state** is a defined status of a specified system or component. States can vary in operation or during projects. A State parameter documents a basic specification qualifier for planning or design, anchoring a scalar measurement or goal level to a particular operational condit

children.name: Value
children.definition: **Value** is perceived benefit: that is, the benefit we think we will, or do, get from something.

children.name: Values
children.definition: **Values** are human culture guidelines that help individuals or groups make choices. They are the principles, standards and paradigms that we consider when choosing alternatives.

children.name: Baseline
children.definition: A Baseline is a stable well-defined benchmark *set* (one or more system attributes) that serve as a comparison for system change.

children.name: Benchmark
children.definition: A benchmark is a specified reference point, or baseline. There are two main types: scalar and binary benchmarks.

children.name: Catastrophe Range Start
children.definition: The exact numeric point where a Catastrophe Range begins.

children.name: Delivered Level
children.definition: For a scalar attribute, the **Delivered Level** is the numeric value on a scale of measure 'delivered' by an Evo step (that is, the resulting level after system enhancement). A Delivered Level is a **Past** benchmark. It is a result of project measurement of progress towards a re

children.name: Delivered Value
children.definition: **Delivered value** is the value delivered by a set of delivery steps to a stakeholder group, as a *consequence* of changing the system attributes.

children.name: Function Baseline
children.definition: A **function baseline** is an analytical statement of system functionality.

children.name: Historic Level
children.definition:
A joint term for the two Benchmark level specifications of attributes, Past and Record.
Note: this does not include Trend and Future, which are benchmarks related to the future and are not in themselves historic.
Source notation: `*084 = {*<Past>. *<Record>}`

children.name: Indicator
children.definition:
An **indicator** is the result of a comparison of a measure or metric with a baseline quantity or expected result.
A Planguage parameter defining an indicator type, and its condition: Example {red light, flashing}.

children.name: Measure of Performance
children.definition: A **Measure of Performance** is a quantitative expression of performance or effectiveness attributes of a system. The Measure of Performance expresses the isolated measurable performance of a system, without respect to its knock-on effects (Measures of Effectiveness *486) in othe

children.name: Past
children.definition: A Past parameter is used to specify historical experience, a 'benchmark'. A Past specification states a historical numeric level, on a defined Scale, under specified conditions [time, place, event] for a scalar attribute.

children.name: Quality Status
children.definition: The **Quality Status** parameter for a specification refers to the official determination of quality approval. Local concepts can be used. Generally the classes are {Not Exited, Exited}. Other possible categories include: Undetermined, Under Revision, Exited, Approved, 'initial,

children.name: Record
children.definition:
A Record parameter is used to inform us about an interesting extreme of achievement.
A Record specification states a benchmark level, on a defined Scale, under specified conditions [time, place, event], for a scalar attribute that represents an impressively good level, or state-o

children.name: Resource Saving
children.definition:
A resource saving is a performance attribute of a system. It expresses 'how much' better the system currently performs in terms of resources than it did at some previous benchmark time.
For example, a resource saving can express how much less resource in training effort or mainte

children.name: Reuse Percentage
children.definition: **Reuse Percentage** is the [defined type of; default = % of volume] percentage of the product development which is accomplished by exploiting the existence of existing components' design or development effort.

children.name: Scalar Baseline
children.definition: A **Scalar Baseline** is a Baseline expressed on a defined scale of measure. It records the current or historical reference-level performance of an attribute as a numeric value on a specified scale, anchoring all subsequent target and constraint specifications.

children.name: Trend
children.definition: A **Trend** parameter is used to specify how we expect or estimate attribute levels to be in the future. It is used as a benchmark.

children.name: Catastrophe Range
children.definition: The catastrophe range is the full numeric extent of all catastrophe levels — the zone beyond the [[Survival.440|Survival]] limit where the system is no longer salvageable.

children.name: Catastrophe
children.definition: A catastrophe level of an attribute is where disaster threatens all, or part, of a system.

children.name: Failure Range
children.definition:
A failure range is a scalar range where some stakeholders will not tolerate the attribute levels. They find the levels unacceptable.
A failure range lies between Acceptable Ranges and Catastrophe Ranges.

children.name: Maximum
children.definition: A **Maximum** specification is a constraint citing the highest allowable numeric level of a scalar variable in the operational variations of a system.

children.name: Minimum
children.definition: A **Minimum** is a constraint specification citing the lowest allowable level of a scalar variable in the operational variations of a system. It is used to define operational characteristics of a system after handover to stakeholders.

children.name: Must Avoid
children.definition:
Must Avoid is a parameter, an abbreviation for the concept 'Fail limit' (*098). It is defined as a level that must be avoided if possible because there is some type and degree of failure at that level and at numerically worse levels.
*See also:* Fail (-ure) Limit *098 — preferred

children.name: OK
children.definition:
The OK point is the level which is, barely, no-longer considered Failure. The OK Range starts just above the Fail level, at the OK Point; and continues until the Goal point level. The dictionary definition of '*satisfactory, but not especially good*', is suitable.
The OK concept

children.name: Performance Constraint
children.definition: A performance constraint specifies some upper and lower limits for an elementary scalar performance attribute. These limits are either levels at which failure of some kind will be experienced, or levels at which the survival of the entire system is threatened. Fail and Survival p

children.name: Performance Survival limit
children.definition: A hard constraint on a scalar performance specified by the Survival limit parameter. Crossing a Performance Survival limit means the continued existence or viability of the entire system is threatened.

children.name: Quality Constraint
children.definition: A **Quality Constraint** sets limits on how bad, or how good, a quality level is allowed to be — on 'how well' the system should perform. When analysing specific stakeholder situations and design costs, a quality constraint may need adjustment or exception when it is violated by

children.name: Survival Range
children.definition: A Survival Range is the numeric range of a scalar attribute that indicates survival of the system, with respect to that attribute alone.

children.name: Tolerable
children.definition: The **Tolerable** level is the project-viability threshold on a scalar attribute scale. Below it, the whole project fails — not just the one attribute value. Above it, the project is still alive. It is the critical boundary that separates the Intolerable Range (project dead) from

children.name: Degree of Target Fulfillment
children.definition: This is the degree, expressed as % of a [qualified] **Target** level (100%), which it has been met, in relation to a defined **Benchmark** level (0%).

children.name: Design Problem
children.keyedIcon: -----<====>----> (the gap between < a past and > a target is an iconic symbol of a design problem)
children.definition: A design problem is expressed as a requirement specification that includes a 'complete set' of valid targets and constraints, together with updated information about the degree of satisfaction in the design or the implementation. A design problem is the 'set of gaps' (to meet req

children.name: Ends
children.definition:
'Ends' is a Planguage parameter that specifies a condition that a defined term has completed successfully (is true).
Usage: to indicate sequential priority in planning time-consuming events such as Evo steps.

children.name: Goal Step
children.definition: A goal step is an intermediate target level on the way to an agreed goal level.

children.name: Performance Target
children.definition: A performance target is a stakeholder-valued, numeric level of system performance. There are three types: a committed planned level (Goal), an uncommitted motivating level (Stretch), and an uncommitted valued level (Wish).

children.name: Quality Requirement
children.definition: A **quality requirement** is a type of performance requirement that deals with 'how good' a system needs to be.

children.name: Quantity Goal
children.definition: **Quantity Goal** is an umbrella class of *performance* goals which covers just about all other goals than those we class as Qualities. Any goal which expresses 'how much' rather than 'how well' is a quantity goal. Quantity goals include {Workload (*459) Goals and Savings (*429)

children.name: Success Range
children.definition: A **Success Range** is meeting the Goal level or better — any measured value at or above the Goal level on a scalar performance scale.

children.name: Target
children.definition: **Targets** are a class of Requirements that we seriously plan to reach.

children.name: Damage
children.definition:
Damage is the negative consequences of successful Attacks to a system. If built-in mitigation fails to deal with attacks, some damage of some sort, by definition, results.
**Gross Damage**: damage remaining after built-in Mitigation (i.e., attacks that succeeded despite it).
**Ne

children.name: Scalability
children.definition: **Scalability** is a system quality that encompasses different types of scaling (such as volume, speed, backup activity, diagnosis activity, and security activity) and different degrees of scaling for defined stakeholders using a defined set of scaling strategies.

children.name: Simple
children.definition: **Simple** is the adjective form of Simplicity (*690): a quantified level of performance, for a defined task, by a defined stakeholder, in a defined environment, that has been achieved or targeted.

children.name: Time To Market
children.definition: The **Time To Market** (TTM) is the calendar time between the [defined] start, or initial staffing, of the project, and the project's [defined level of] product successful release to [defined] market. A scale of measure.

children.name: Workload Capacity Requirement
children.definition: A **Workload Capacity Requirement** is a need to achieve specific work capability levels for a system: 'how much' work a system should do.

children.name: Workload Capacity
children.definition: **Workload Capacity** is a performance attribute. It is used to express the capacity of a system to carry out its workload, that is 'how much' a system can do, did, or will do.

children.name: Incremental Scale Impact
children.definition:
For a scalar requirement, this is the numeric impact of a design idea *relative* to the specified baseline level. If there is a negative impact, then the numeric value will be negative.
**Scale Impact − Baseline = Incremental Scale Impact**

children.name: Scale Context
children.definition: A **Scale Context** is all the additional information that applies to a Scale of Measure, in addition to the units of measure. It includes qualifiers, conditions, definitions, and any other specification elements that make the scale precisely applicable to a specific measurement

children.name: Scale Impact
children.definition: A **Scale Impact** is an absolute numeric value on the scale of measure for a scalar requirement. It represents the level estimated or actually achieved when a specified design idea (or set of design ideas, or Evo Step) is implemented — including all effects of previously impleme

children.name: Scale Qualifier Conditions
children.definition: **Scale Qualifier Conditions** are Qualifier Conditions (*666) embedded within a defined Scale of Measure. They are the specific qualifier conditions that a Scale Qualifier (*381) introduces into the scale definition — conditions that must be explicitly bound (by a Scale Qualifie

children.name: Scale Qualifier Definition
children.definition: A **Scale Qualifier Definition** is the specific term assigned to finally define a qualifier condition for a corresponding Scale Qualifier. For example, in `Scale: time to complete a defined [Task]`, the Scale Qualifier is `[Task]` and `Update` is a Scale Qualifier Definition whe

children.name: Scale Qualifier
children.definition: A **Scale Qualifier** is an optional term within the *definition* of a Scale of Measure that defines generic conditions — such as `[Task]` or `[Stakeholder]` — that must be specifically assigned (bound) in any parameter statement that references the Scale. Scale Qualifiers make s

children.name: Scale Type
children.definition: A **scale type** is a classification of the mathematical structure of a scale of measure — for example, whether the scale uses ordinal ranking, interval measurement, or ratio measurement with a true zero.

children.name: Scale Uncertainty
children.definition: A **scale uncertainty** is an estimate of the error margins for a specific scale impact — the plus-and-minus range on the scale of measure over which an impact estimate can possibly vary — allowing calculation of best-case and worst-case borders.

children.name: Scale of Measure
children.definition: A **scale of measure** defines a single scalar attribute dimension — the common reference framework against which all numeric levels (benchmarks, goals, constraints, estimates) for that attribute are expressed.

children.name: Units Context
children.definition: A **Units Context** defines where the scale of measure is applicable. It primarily contains place, space, event; secondarily contains sources, authority, priority.

children.name: Units Qualifier
children.definition: **Units Qualifiers** specify in a Scale of measure which dimensions apply to the units of measure.

children.name: Units of Measure
children.definition: **Units of Measure** define the basic units to be used for measurement in a scale of measure.

children.name: Context
children.definition: A context is a system view from any useful perspective.

children.name: Global
children.definition: 'Global' is an adjective used to specify that something applies to all (each individual component) of the set of components within the specified scope.

children.name: Host System
children.definition: A host system receives the evolutionary *delivery steps*.

children.name: Place
children.definition: 'Place' defines '*where*'. It relates to any notion of place, such as geographic location, stakeholder role, customer market, or system component. Place is used both as a parameter and in a qualifier condition.

children.name: Process Language
children.definition: The subset of Planguage (or of a specific Project Language), which describes work activities. It is used to specify the process descriptions that utilize, or produce, the information expressed when using the Specification Language and Product Language.

children.name: Project Language
children.definition: The set of all Process Language, Product Language and Specification Language artifacts used by a defined project.

children.name: Scope
children.definition: A **scope** describes the extent of influence of something — a specification, a system, a project, or any other defined entity — expressed using Planguage qualifiers (time, place, event, stakeholder, etc.) or any other useful terms.

children.name: Space
children.definition: **Space** is a specification concept that encompasses the geographic 'Place' notion and, in addition, any other *notions of group or location* — such as component, market, religion, race, or organisational unit. It refers to the set of possible scope dimensions that are neither t

children.name: Specific
children.definition: **Specific** means applicable to a precise, definite set of components. It is usually used to reduce scope to declare a component (or set of components) as being explicitly singled out as the subject for attention. A *specific constraint* is a system specification constraint that

children.name: System Container
children.definition: **System Container** is any physical or conceptual system component which physically or logically serves as an interface to a defined set of system components.

children.name: Time
children.definition: **Time** defines 'when'. It relates to any notion of time: clock-time or timescale.

children.name: Derivative Source
children.definition: The source of the Derived (*449) specification or plan. The 'source' implies the resource and the rule for conversion into the derivative.

children.name: Master Definition
children.definition: The **Master Definition** of a specification, or specification element, is the primary and authoritative source of information about its meaning. The master definition overrides any other (informal, not master) definition that is in conflict with it.

children.name: Master Term
children.definition: A **Master Term** is the primary, or only, reference tag to a master definition (*303).

children.name: Source
children.definition: **Source** is a synonym for process input *information* (as opposed to process input *materials*). In SQC workflows, source specifications are contained in documents that are usually of earlier production — and typically at higher levels of authority, global scope, and abstractio

children.name: Specification Reference
children.definition: A **Specification Reference** is any user-defined Tag which cross-references a defined term elsewhere in the specification. This does not include Planguage parameters.

children.name: Parameter
children.definition: A parameter is a Planguage-defined term. Parameters are always written with at least a leading capital letter, to signal the existence of a formal definition.

children.name: QC Parameter
children.definition: QC Parameter is the taxonomy class for parameters used in Quality Control work (Defect, Sample, Major Defect, Root Cause, Inspection metrics, etc.). It groups the *language* side of Quality Control — the terms used to describe defect work — separate from the *enacted* QC Process.

children.name: Absolute Specification
children.definition: An absolute specification of a term can be understood fully without reference to other definitions.

children.name: Architecture Specification
children.definition: An architecture specification is the written definition of an architectural component.

children.name: Kickoff
children.definition: Kickoff is an SQC sub-process. It usually involves a team meeting to agree on the master plan, and to commit to doing the planned SQC work.

children.name: Planning
children.definition: **Planning [SQC]** (*284) is the opening sub-process of Specification Quality Control. An SQC team leader produces a 'master plan' for the quality control of a specific 'main specification.' The planning session lasts approximately one hour and involves completing a Master Plan f

children.name: Report [SQC]
children.definition: A 'report' is an *oral* statement made during SQC at a specification meeting or a process meeting.

children.name: Specification Meeting
children.definition: A **Specification Meeting** is an SQC sub-process — a meeting of checkers and a team leader, scheduled after the individual Checking sub-process. Its overall purpose is to evaluate the results from the individual checking activity and to produce an Editor Advice Log as written ou

children.name: Specification Review Rule
children.definition: A **Specification Review Rule** specifies the official known best practices for deriving a systems engineering concept (for example, a design) from other information (such as requirements and known technology). A specification review rule is used both to instruct the engineer in

children.name: System Definition Rule
children.definition: A **system definition rule** is any statement which specifies a rule of any kind for the design or action of any system.

children.name: Client Stakeholder
children.definition: A Client Stakeholder states needs, approves requirements and receives benefits or results produced by a Server Stakeholder.

children.name: Client
children.definition: A client is a person or group who has requested some defined work, system, or product, and will pay for it, directly or indirectly.

children.name: Consumer
children.definition: A consumer is a person or group who makes use of ('consumes') a process output (product).

children.name: Decision-maker
children.definition: A decision-maker is a person or group who will make a specific defined decision. Also referred to as a decision-taker.

children.name: External Stakeholder
children.definition:
External stakeholders are stakeholders which are directly impacted by, or which use, a defined focus system.
For example: a product customer or user is an external stakeholder in relation to that product (a defined focus system).

children.name: Funder
children.definition: One who provides money, or other resources, for a project.

children.name: Internal Stakeholder
children.definition: Internal stakeholders are stakeholders that directly impact a defined focus system. They are related to the environment systems supporting the focus system. For example, a tester is an internal stakeholder for a test process supporting the development of a product (defined as a f

children.name: Potential Consumer
children.definition: A **Potential Consumer** is an organization, or individual, which does not presently use or pay for a defined system {product, Evo step, service, process} but who might consider doing so.

children.name: Recipient
children.definition: An Evo delivery step recipient. A host system user, a customer, a client, a consumer, a stakeholder, a market or any people or instances that are the target, or potential target, of an Evo step delivery.

children.name: Server Stakeholder
children.definition: A **server stakeholder** is a stakeholder who attempts to deliver results in order to satisfy the needs of a client stakeholder.

children.name: Sponsor
children.definition: A **sponsor** is a person or group who has an interest in supporting the achievement of specific system change — and who contributes, or is willing to contribute, resources toward that achievement. Resources can include financial budget, people, materials, reputation, or vocal/po

children.name: User
children.definition: A **user** is a person or group, who actually will make practical use of a system.

children.name: Checklist
children.definition: A checklist is a list of items to be checked or verified, used as a standard to guide quality control processes and reviews.

children.name: Concept
children.definition: A concept is an idea.

children.name: Form
children.definition: A **form** is a written document (electronic or paper) that guides people to give specific data with specific content in specific formats, in specific presentation sequences. It is a 'work process standard' for data collection. It is also an implicit 'procedure' for data collecti

children.name: Generic Standard
children.definition: A 'generic' standard is an example, model, specification, form, or template of a work process standard, which can then be tailored, or applied without tailoring, by their user to suit their purposes.

children.name: Guideline
children.definition: A guideline is a specific written piece of advice, a recommendation, a tip, a hint, a suggestion, or a warning. It can be found in a specification, but is often placed into a set of guidelines, which are more widely available (sometimes held alongside the standards documentation)

children.name: Policy
children.definition: A **policy** is a set of principles for decision-making, which permit delegation of decision-making to other people, at other times, under 'unknown conditions at the time of writing the policy'. However, policy may be ignored for higher priority considerations. For example, becau

children.name: Procedure
children.definition: A **procedure** is a repeatable description to instruct people as to the best-known practice, or recommended way, to carry out the task, of a defined process.

children.name: Rate
children.definition: **Rate** refers to the defined speed with which a defined task is carried out, per defined unit-of-volume worked on. Rates can be set as process standards. This implies that adjustment of rates of work towards more effective or optimum rate-levels is something that can be 'learne

children.name: Review Criteria
children.definition: **Review Criteria** are the rules (and related checklists), the defined procedures, and any other standards or guidelines to be used to define and direct the analysis process, for a particular review activity. They are the questions the reviewers must ask and answer. They are the

children.name: Rule
children.definition: **Rule *609** is a type of Standard (*138) in the Standards hierarchy, as extracted from the hierarchy diagram in the Planguage source (PDF p.379). Its sub-types include: Generic Specification Rule, Concept Rule, Policy Rule, Process Rule, Process Structure, Specification Rule, a

children.name: Process Description
children.definition: A process description is a process definition. It consists of the following components: {entry conditions, procedure, exit conditions}. The process description must also reference any rules that apply.

children.name: Rule
children.definition: A **Rule** is any statement of a standard on how to write or carry out some part of a systems engineering or business process.

children.name: Standard
children.definition: A **standard** is an official, written specification that guides a defined group of people in doing a process. It is a best-known practice. Standards include: {rule, policy, process, entry condition, procedure, exit condition, form, template}.

children.name: Dynamic
children.definition:
Dynamic means something happening in real time.
**Antonyms:** Passive · Static

children.name: Status
children.definition: A **Status** level is the current scalar value of an attribute being tracked as a system evolves — the last known measured level on a defined Scale of Measure, at a defined point in time, space, and event condition.

children.name: On
children.definition: **On** is a predefined State value. **On** is the same as True (*625). It represents the binary "active / true" condition of a two-state system attribute.

children.name: Changing
children.definition: Predefined State. The state is in continuous but predictable flux, not stable.

children.name: Confidentiality
children.definition: The level of readership to which a specification is restricted.

children.name: Default
children.definition: A **Default** specification is a term to be used as a value when none is explicitly specified.

children.name: Explicit Parameters
children.definition: Parameters in a specification that are defined by *direct use* of their defined parameter name.

children.name: Fuzzy
children.definition: A specification, which is known to be somewhat unclear, potentially incorrect or incomplete, is called 'fuzzy'. It should be clearly declared as 'fuzzy'. The keyed icons '< >' are used to explicitly mark any fuzzy specifications.

children.name: High-Level
children.definition:
'High-level' refers to a position that is 'high' (that is, closer to the top than the bottom) in any specified hierarchy of system components.
Since a given hierarchy can be made using any arbitrary top and bottom notions, the reference applies only to a given hierarchy, and is n

children.name: Operational
children.definition: **Operational** refers to a state of defined systems in defined states of operation. It is used as a qualifier for Requirements, Attributes, and Functions: Operational Requirements, Operational Attributes, Operational Functions — each referring to the set that applies to the syst

children.name: Option
children.definition: An **Option** is a short form of "template option." It defines optional parameters or qualifiers in a model or a template for Planguage. An Option is indicated by placing the parameter name in parentheses `( )` in the template definition — showing that it may be omitted in any gi

children.name: Problem
children.definition: A question to be considered, solved or answered.

children.name: Proposal
children.definition: A suggestion to be considered, evaluated, analyzed, estimated before becoming accepted, approved or considered valid. A proposal can be put forward orally, by specification, or be implied in some other formulation as a consequence ('let us stick with the current design' implies w

children.name: Prototype
children.definition: A **prototype** is any design implementation made with one primary objective: to get feedback from stakeholders, including collection of data about costs and quality levels, for that technology or design, for those stakeholders. A prototype reflects only conceptual design decisio

children.name: Significant Specification
children.definition: **Significant Specification** refers to any specification content which, if wrong, misinterpreted, or missing, represents a potential for non-trivial downstream cost to correct and suffer.

children.name: Specification Maturity
children.definition: **Specification Maturity** is the level of evolution of a specification, standard, or process artefact. It is a parameter used to describe how far along the lifecycle a specification has progressed, and is explicitly *not* a measure of specification quality.

children.name: Undeterminable
children.definition: **Undeterminable** is a predefined State. Attempt to determine has been made and the result is no clear state information is available.

children.name: Undetermined
children.definition: **Undetermined** is a predefined State. The state determination has either not been attempted or is not concluded yet.

children.name: Unknown
children.definition: **Unknown** is a predefined State. The state is not known.

children.name: Unstable
children.definition: **Unstable** is a predefined State. The state is changing in unpredictable ways.

children.name: Abstract Strategy
children.definition: An abstract strategy is an idea or state, without itself containing or being a [[Concrete-Strategy.661|Concrete Strategy]] (*661).

children.name: Concrete Strategy
children.definition: A concrete strategy [is] any device or means for supporting specified aims, which is existing in a real or material form, and is not abstract.

children.name: Evo Plan
children.definition: An Evo plan is a set of sequenced and/or a set of yet-to-be sequenced Evo steps. The current planned sequence of delivery of any of the steps should be reconsidered after each Evo step has actually been delivered, and the feedback has been analyzed. Many factors, internal and ext

children.name: Drawn Icon
children.definition:
A drawn icon is a defined graphic symbol, or pictorial representation of a Planguage concept, constructed by drawing, rather than keying.
**Note:** Keyed Icons are a sub-class of icons constructed entirely by keying keyboard symbols. Drawn Icons require drawing tools rather than

children.name: Generic Attribute Level Icon
children.definition: A neutral graphic symbol, `(---|---)`, for a numeric level of a performance or cost attribute. The Generic symbol is used in place of unknown, undetermined or uninteresting specific symbols of attribute priority or character; such as any Benchmark (example `---<<--`) or Target (e

children.name: Icon
children.definition: In Planguage, an icon is a symbol, keyed (Keyed Icon) or drawn (Drawn Icon), that represents a concept. All Icons are graphic or pictorial in nature — they should not use words or national languages. But they can be annotated by words or symbols. They refer specifically to define

children.name: Keyed Icon
children.definition: A keyed icon is a non-alphabetic and non-mnemonic set of one or more key-able characters that make up a keyed icon symbol, with defined interpretation. The choice of keyed characters is as closely related as possible to the corresponding icon, and ideally is acceptable to all lan

children.name: Symbol
children.definition: A **Symbol** is any defined representation of information, concrete realities, or abstractions such as emotion.

children.name: Backroom
children.definition: Backroom is an adjective or noun, referring to a conceptual place, used to describe any processes or activities in Evo that are not necessarily visible to the Evo step recipients.

children.name: Black Box
children.definition: A Black Box is a conceptual interface to any system of perhaps unknown, or unknowable, internal complexity and/or construction.

children.name: Domain
children.definition:
A domain is a major field of influence or responsibility for a defined subject.
**Standards comparison (Webster's):** "A field or sphere of activity or influence."

children.name: Environment System
children.definition: An environment system is any system related to a defined Focus System. For example it could be a development process or development tool for a product (designated as the defined focus system).

children.name: External
children.definition: When describing the relationship amongst objects, **External** is an adjective which applies to any object outside the scope of a given object.

children.name: Focus System
children.definition:
A focus system is the system, or product, we have decided to focus our attention on. All other systems related to it are 'Environment' systems.
The purpose of this concept is to allow us to define a focus on one particular element of a set of related systems.
For example if we ar

children.name: Frontroom
children.definition: **Frontroom** is an adjective or noun, referring to a conceptual place, used to describe any project management processes or activities, in Evo, that are visible to the Evo step recipients.

children.name: Internal
children.definition: When describing the relationship amongst objects, 'internal' is an adjective which applies to any object inside the scope of a given object.

children.name: System
children.definition: A **system** is any useful subset of the universe that we choose to specify. It can be conceptual or real.

children.name: Target System
children.definition: A **Target System** is a defined system that is the target of a defined change effort by an agent system.

children.name: Function
children.definition:
A **function** is 'what' a system does.
A function is a binary concept, and is always expressed in action ('to do') terms (for example, 'to span a gap' and 'to manage a process').

children.name: System Element
children.definition: System Element is the taxonomy class for things-in-the-system (as opposed to specifications about the system). Sub-groups: System Boundary, Partitioning, Component & Object, Software & Technology Material, Agent & Mechanism, System Property, Lifecycle Phase.

children.name: Agent System
children.definition: An **Agent System** is the entity — organisation, team, process, or programme — that is responsible for directing deliberate change at a [[Target-System.610|Target System]] (*610). The Agent System drives the change; the Target System is what changes.

children.name: Planguage Concept
children.definition: A **Planguage Concept** (*188) is a formally specified idea used in Planguage. Planguage is defined formally in Gilb: *Competitive Engineering* [2005, Elsevier]. www.Gilb.com contains samples and many related papers.

children.name: Assertion
children.definition: An assertion is a statement that something is true, without necessarily backing it up with evidence or proof.

children.name: Attribute Level Icon Point
children.definition: The exact point in space, in a diagram, which represents a given attribute level.

children.name: Attribute
children.definition: An attribute is an observable characteristic of a system.

children.name: Benefit
children.definition: Benefit is value delivered to stakeholders.

children.name: Binary
children.definition: Binary is an adjective used to describe objects, which are specified as observable in two states.

children.name: Business Rules
children.definition: Business Rules are specifications or practices that define or constrain some aspect or principle of how a business operates or should operate — its 'rules of behavior'.

children.name: Control Chart
children.definition: "A control chart is a graphic comparison of process performance data to computed 'control limits' drawn as limit lines on the chart." [JURAN74]

children.name: Control Limits
children.definition: Control limits are the upper and lower bounds on a control chart. Control limits should contain, within those boundaries, all observations of 'variation due to common causes'. Observations *outside* the control limits are *probably* due to special causes.

children.name: Control Point
children.definition:
Control points are the specified elements that must be considered in solving a problem. They include requirements, constraints, qualifiers, and inherited specification elements.
The number of problem control points that must be considered is a measure of the complexity of the pro

children.name: Controllability
children.definition:
A component of the system state vector is **Controllable** if there exists a control signal which can bring the system from the current state to a desired state.
It is **Observable** if it is possible to compute or estimate the state from a finitely long observation of the system

children.name: Controllable
children.definition: *Controllable* is the type of objective where the Design Ideas chosen are capable of influencing Fundamental Objectives at all.

children.name: Core Ideology
children.definition: Core Ideology consists of Core Purpose and Core Values.

children.name: Core Values
children.definition: Core Values are a handful of basic ingrained beliefs about how to run a given organisation. They are almost unchangeable for the lifetime of the organisation. They are the strongest guidelines that all other activity in the organisation must try to align with. They are the highes

children.name: Culture
children.definition: "Culture is an umbrella term which encompasses the social behavior, institutions, and norms found in human societies, as well as the knowledge, beliefs, arts, laws, customs, capabilities, and habits of the individuals in these groups. Culture is often originated from or attribute

children.name: Derivative
children.definition: The thing derived from its Derivative Source (*450). The source is the initial information or resource, and some rules or process for derivation.

children.name: Derived
children.definition: Something resulting from processing other information according to defined rules. A derived requirement is a specific requirement obtained by applying a generic requirement to a local range.

children.name: Descendant
children.definition:
An artifact descended from another artifact; immediately, or via several levels of process.
A Kid is always a descendant of a Parent. A design could be the descendant of a set of requirements.

children.name: Feedback
children.definition:
Any form of information, about a defined event, which could potentially be used by any stakeholder, for any set of defined purposes.
**Form of Information:** defined: any sound, picture, text, event, etc., related to the 'Defined Feedback Causal Event', which can be captured, ana

children.name: Gaming
children.definition: Conscious manipulation of requirements or evaluations so as to achieve special aims.

children.name: Input/output axis
children.definition: The vertical axis of a process rectangle. The top represents inputs to the process (data and/or material) — *DE* (Data Entry) below. The bottom represents outputs from the process (data and/or material) — *DX* (Data Exit) below. Abbreviation: I/O Axis. Not coincidentally, the top

children.name: Intelligible
children.definition: Capable of being understood.

children.name: Level of Perception
children.definition: The 'Level of Perception' is the organisational or process level which a specification is at or related to. For example, the architectural level is downstream of system level requirements level but is upstream of specialist engineering levels.

children.name: Monster
children.definition:
A new ambition level above Stretch. Syntax: `Monster: Scale 100 × Goal { if available, then capture }`
Example: Goal: 5,000 Model 3 / week · Stretch: 7,500 / week · Monster: 20,000 / week `{ if demand and supply both exceed forecasts by 3σ }`.

children.name: Motivating
children.definition:
A 'motivating' systems component is one which causes people to act.
**Formally:** Motivating [defined Systems Component] is a cause of defined [Stakeholders] for doing defined [Actions].
**Usage 1. Motivating Needs:** the stakeholder needs which cause them to fund or otherwise su

children.name: Objectivity
children.definition: **Objectivity** means being independent of subjective influences — a reality outside individual minds, closer to some real truth independent of the observer's person or culture.

children.name: Observability
children.definition: **Observability** is the property of a system component (a state variable) such that it is possible to compute or estimate that component's state from a finitely long observation of the system's outputs. The generic term "observable" covers any means of observing a system: testin

children.name: Open-Ended
children.definition: **Open-Ended** means that a system's architecture — its interfaces and basic structure — is of such a nature that most system changes, no matter how unexpected, are relatively easy to handle without major effort. The more open-ended, the easier the change will probably be.

children.name: Pattern
children.definition: A 'Pattern' is a general tool that defines any idea structure, or sets of structures, in any intelligible format, which can be exploited by tailoring it to, or copying it into, a specific domain. Patterns are a form of stored wisdom or knowledge. The main idea is to allow people

children.name: Philosophy
children.definition: "A basic theory concerning a particular subject." (*The American Heritage Dictionary, Dell.*) In Planguage usage: "The set of values of an individual culture." Planguage is based on the central idea that quantification of multiple critical quality values is basic to controlling r

children.name: Pragmatic
children.definition: A **'pragmatic'** is a device for getting something done, which is more *practical* than theoretical. We do not have to understand why or how it works, only know that it probably works. This would not satisfy a scientist, but is useful in engineering. Heuristics are pragmatics.

children.name: Principle
children.definition: A **principle** is a short basic statement which summarizes and teaches basic philosophy or the pragmatics of a method.

children.name: Problem Definition
children.definition: A **problem definition** is a statement of a problem that implicitly needs one or more solution options.

children.name: Productivity
children.definition: Productivity is **delivering promised value to stakeholders**. 'Deliver' means actually measurable handed over and available to stakeholders. 'Promised' means that clear written agreements, are made in contacts, requirements, documents and slides, or clear undeniable expectations

children.name: Profession
children.definition: An individual activity specialization requiring considerable training and/or experience. Examples: planner, engineer, quality control manager, project manager, top manager, supervisor, field worker of various types.

children.name: Subjectivity
children.definition: **Subjectivity** is that which is predominantly a matter of personal opinion, or taste, or state of mind.

children.name: System Descriptor
children.definition: A **system descriptor** is any external or internal attribute {performance, quality, cost, function, constraint, design or other notion} which is used in some way to describe or characterize a system.

children.name: Systemic
children.definition: **Systemic** means 'of', or 'relating to', the entire system.

children.name: Ultimotive
children.definition: An **ultimotive** is the highest level of motivation in a defined chain of motivations.

children.name: Basic Planguage
children.definition: Basic Planguage is the original specification of Planguage — the generic, un-tailored form of the language, as opposed to project-specific tailored variants.

children.name: Data
children.definition: Data is any form of signal which humans or machines can *usefully* distinguish from other signals. Data is interpreted by some sensing agent, a reader, or a computer, which tries to convert it into useful information. Data can be viewed as a necessary system resource, and also as

children.name: Dataware
children.definition: Dataware includes any data which can be or is in fact processed by a computer.

children.name: Diagram
children.definition: A set of icons, symbols and terms, which pictorially explains how something works, or tries to clarify the relationship between parts of the whole.

children.name: Document
children.definition: A document is a readable instrument for containing and conveying ideas of any kind.

children.name: Documentation
children.definition: Documentation is written information that teaches people how to use systems.

children.name: Handbook Variant
children.definition: A variation of the Planguage Handbook made for a particular organization, or language.

children.name: Impact Estimation Table
children.definition: An **impact estimation table** (IE table) is the main output specification of an Impact Estimation process. An IE table shows estimates or actual measurements of the effect of any set of designs (architecture, strategy, solution) on any set of requirements. The emphasis is on the

children.name: Information
children.definition: Information is the interpretation an agent gives to data.

children.name: Infoware
children.definition: Infoware encompasses any *devices* for informing *people* about *ideas*. Infoware is information carriers in the widest sense of the word. This includes anything people can read (text, diagrams, pictures) and any real artefacts which people can learn something from such as: model

children.name: Knowledge
children.definition: Facts, information, and skills *accessible* by a system *stakeholder* by any *means*; for the theoretical or practical understanding of a subject.

children.name: Logicware
children.definition: Any information which is intended to control the logical action of a computer. This includes the obvious — computer programs (logic itself) — including any data that in fact controls the computer logic, such as user parameters which control computer logic, and data integrated int

children.name: Logistics
children.definition: The procurement, distribution, maintenance, and replacement of materiel and personnel.

children.name: Model
children.definition:
A model is an artificial representation of an idea or a product. The representation can be in any useful format including specifications, drawings and physical representations.
Rationale: to convey information about an idea without having to deal with a full scale and real versio

children.name: Planware
children.definition: **Planware** is any specification, intent or agreement, which documents or reveals human intentions, and perhaps the background and status for those intentions. In simpler words, any plans of any kind. It does not have to be written.

children.name: Softect
children.definition: A **Softect** is one who does software or IT systems architecture — a concatenation of *software* and *architect*.

children.name: Software
children.definition: **Software** refers to the 'non-hardware' aspects or components of a system. It specifically includes computer programs, data (computer-readable files and databases), and software documentation and plans (any form of specification or plans made by people concerning software).

children.name: Systect
children.definition: A **Systect** is a person who does Systecture (systems architecture) — a systems architect. It is a conjunction (systems architect).

children.name: Technology
children.definition: **Technology** is the methods and materials used to construct or modify a system. The design ideas and functionality.

children.name: After
children.definition: 'After' is a parameter used to indicate a planned sequencing of events, including [[Evo-Step.141|Evo steps]] and [[Task.149|tasks]].

children.name: Before
children.definition: 'Before' is a parameter used to indicate planned sequencing of events, including Evo steps and tasks.

children.name: Due
children.definition:
'Due' is a specification parameter indicating when some aspect of a specification is due.
**Historical note:** "The idea of 'Due' as a parameter was from an unpublished note by Jens Weber, Daimler Chrysler, Frankfurt."

children.name: During
children.keyedIcon: ||  as in A||B  (A is done in parallel with B)
children.definition:
'During' is a specification parameter used when specifying events (including Evo steps and tasks) to indicate a time dependency for events that must be carried out concurrently (that is, done in parallel).
**Keyed icon:** `||` as in `A||B` — "A is done in parallel with B."

children.name: Milestone
children.definition: A **Milestone** is any defined measure of project progress. In Evolutionary Project Management, the successful completion of Evo steps is the normal milestone concept. But any set of Evo steps (Mega-steps) can be used to define interesting milestones.

children.name: Mode
children.definition: A mode is a defined type of operation of a system.

children.name: Precedes
children.definition: **'Precedes'** gives information about required sequential *evaluation* of Planguage statements, terms or expressions, in relation to one another. It is implied that the result of the evaluation of any preceding statement or expression, must be applied to the following Planguage

children.name: Starts
children.definition: **Starts** indicates the condition where a defined event begins. It marks only the initiation boundary of an event — it says nothing about duration, whether the event is still in progress, or whether it has been completed.

children.name: Percentage Uncertainty
children.definition:
Percentage uncertainty is calculated from the scale uncertainty, baseline and target data; and stated together with the percentage impact value.
Percentage Uncertainty can be used to identify risks in using specific design ideas: the numeric 'best case' and 'worst case' deviation

children.name: Aim
children.definition: An 'aim' is a stated desire to achieve something by certain stakeholders. An aim is usually specified informally and non-numerically.

children.name: Ambition
children.definition:
'Ambition' is a parameter, which can be used to summarize the ambition *level* of a performance or budget target requirement.
Ambition must state the requirement concerned (like 'Usability') and it must contain a notion of the kind of level being sought (like 'high').

children.name: Cycle Priority
children.definition: The calculated relative (to other potential cycles) importance of a specific planned evolutionary delivery cycle.

children.name: Objective Function
children.definition: "An objective function maps future sequences of states of the world to the value they have for specific stakeholders, in utility terms. Objective functions have various inputs from which to derive an overall utility value. The inputs can be called the dimensions of the objective

children.name: Priority Signal
children.definition: **Priority signals** are any specification attributes — local, in the environment, or inherited — which can be used to determine the priority (claim on limited resources) of one specification over others.

children.name: Priority
children.definition: **Priority** is a parameter used to indicate the relative importance or ordering of requirements, design elements, or other specification items. The keyed icons `>`, `<`, `=` are used to express relative priority relationships: `>` means higher priority than; `<` means lower prio

children.name: Purpose
children.definition: **Purpose** is the reason something exists, has been done, or is made.

children.name: Ultimate
children.definition: The systems engineering component, at the highest level worthy of consideration, is the **ultimate** component.

children.name: View
children.definition: A **view** is any useful perspective regarding a defined system.

children.name: Viewpoint
children.definition: A **Viewpoint** captures the rules for constructing and analyzing a particular kind of view. It is a template for a view and can be reused across many architecture descriptions.

children.name: Vision
children.definition: A **Vision** is an idea about a future state, which is very long range, and probably idealistic, maybe even unrealistic.

children.name: Checking Rate
children.definition: The checking rate is the *average* speed at which a specification is checked by a checker, using all the relevant related specifications and standards {the main specification, rules, checklists, source documents and kin documents}.

children.name: Optimum Checking Rate
children.definition: The **Optimum Checking Rate** is the average rate of checking a specification that gives the highest productivity (effectiveness). It is usually measured as the number of pages or lines per hour at which the peak ability to identify major defects per page is achieved.
